drugs.indications: Induction of intraoperative miosis during cataract surgery
drugs.mechanism: Binds and activates muscarinic (M1-M5) and nicotinic receptors, mimicking endogenous acetylcholine; rapidly hydrolyzed by acetylcholinesterase so has almost no systemic duration
drugs.metabolism: Hydrolyzed almost instantly by acetylcholinesterase and plasma pseudocholinesterase

drugs.therapeuticClass: Direct-acting muscarinic/nicotinic agonist, resistant to acetylcholinesterase
drugs.indications: Glaucoma (intraocular pressure reduction), intraoperative miosis
drugs.mechanism: Direct muscarinic and nicotinic agonist; not hydrolyzed by acetylcholinesterase, giving a longer duration than acetylcholine itself

drugs.indications: Postoperative/postpartum non-obstructive urinary retention, neurogenic bladder
drugs.mechanism: Selective M3 muscarinic agonist, resistant to acetylcholinesterase; increases detrusor muscle contraction and GI motility
drugs.metabolism: Resistant to cholinesterase; minimal hepatic metabolism

drugs.indications: Glaucoma (open/closed-angle), xerostomia (Sjögren's syndrome, post-radiation)
drugs.mechanism: Direct muscarinic agonist causing miosis and ciliary muscle contraction, opening trabecular meshwork to increase aqueous outflow; oral form stimulates salivary/sweat gland secretion

dosing.standard: 1-2 drops of 0.5-4% solution or 5mg oral tablet

drugs.indications: Glaucoma, presbyopia (newer indication for pupil constriction)
drugs.mechanism: Direct muscarinic agonist producing miosis and increased aqueous outflow, similar to pilocarpine but with reportedly less accommodative spasm

drugs.indications: Organophosphate poisoning (insecticides, nerve agents) as adjunct to atropine
drugs.mechanism: Reactivates acetylcholinesterase inhibited by organophosphates by breaking the phosphate-enzyme bond, before 'aging' occurs (irreversible bond)

dosing.frequency: Single dose, may repeat or infuse

drugs.clinicalPearls: Must be given before 'aging' of the enzyme-organophosphate complex occurs (varies by agent, can be within hours) — delayed administration is far less effective.

drugs.indications: Symptomatic bradycardia, organophosphate/cholinergic toxicity, preoperative antisialagogue, mydriasis for eye exams
drugs.mechanism: Competitive antagonist at all 5 muscarinic receptor subtypes, blocking parasympathetic effects; increases heart rate, dries secretions, dilates pupils

drugs.therapeuticClass: Non-selective muscarinic antagonist with CNS penetration
drugs.indications: Motion sickness prevention, postoperative nausea/vomiting prophylaxis
drugs.mechanism: Crosses blood-brain barrier to block muscarinic receptors in the vestibular system and vomiting center, unlike atropine which is more peripherally restricted

drugs.indications: COPD, asthma (adjunct), allergic/vasomotor rhinitis (nasal spray)
drugs.mechanism: Blocks M3 muscarinic receptors in bronchial smooth muscle, reducing bronchoconstriction; quaternary ammonium structure limits systemic/CNS absorption
drugs.elimination: Renal and biliary (unabsorbed drug in feces)
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to atropine derivatives or soy/peanut (some formulations)

drugs.indications: COPD maintenance therapy, asthma (add-on)
drugs.mechanism: Long-acting M3 selective antagonist with slow dissociation from receptors, providing 24-hour bronchodilation

dosing.standard: 18 mcg (dry powder) or 2.5 mcg x2 (soft mist)

drugs.indications: Mydriasis and cycloplegia for fundoscopic/refraction eye exams
drugs.mechanism: Blocks iris sphincter and ciliary muscle muscarinic receptors, causing rapid pupil dilation and cycloplegia with shorter duration than atropine

dosing.maxDose: Repeat once after 5 min if needed

drugs.indications: Cycloplegic refraction, particularly in pediatric patients
drugs.mechanism: Blocks ciliary muscle muscarinic receptors producing cycloplegia and mydriasis, longer duration than tropicamide but shorter than atropine
sideEffects: CNS effects in children (disorientation, ataxia — crosses BBB more than tropicamide)
drugs.metabolism: Systemic absorption possible via nasolacrimal duct

drugs.indications: Drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms (acute dystonia, parkinsonism from antipsychotics), adjunct in Parkinson's disease
drugs.mechanism: Blocks central muscarinic receptors, restoring dopamine-acetylcholine balance in the basal ganglia disrupted by dopamine-blocking antipsychotics

dosing.standard: 1-2 mg IV/IM for acute dystonia; 1-4 mg/day oral maintenance

drugs.indications: Parkinson's disease (tremor-predominant), drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms
drugs.mechanism: Central antimuscarinic action rebalancing striatal dopamine-acetylcholine ratio, particularly effective for tremor

drugs.indications: Overactive bladder, urge urinary incontinence, neurogenic detrusor overactivity
drugs.mechanism: Blocks M3 muscarinic receptors on detrusor smooth muscle, reducing involuntary bladder contractions and increasing bladder capacity

dosing.standard: 5 mg oral 2-3x daily or 10 mg ER once daily

drugs.indications: Hypotension (especially anesthesia-induced), nasal decongestion, mydriasis, orthostatic hypotension
drugs.mechanism: Direct, selective agonist at alpha1-adrenergic receptors causing vasoconstriction, increasing systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure without significant beta-adrenergic (chronotropic) effect

dosing.frequency: IV boluses as needed or infusion

drugs.indications: Hypotension during anesthesia, paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (historically, via reflex vagal response)
drugs.mechanism: Pure alpha1 agonist causing vasoconstriction and reflex bradycardia via baroreceptor response, with no direct cardiac stimulation

drugs.indications: Orthostatic hypotension (neurogenic)
drugs.mechanism: Prodrug converted to active metabolite desglymidodrine, a selective alpha1 agonist causing arterial and venous vasoconstriction, raising standing blood pressure
drugs.metabolism: Hepatic and intestinal conversion to active metabolite

drugs.indications: Nasal congestion, ocular redness (allergic/irritant conjunctivitis)
drugs.mechanism: Direct alpha1/alpha2 agonist causing local vasoconstriction, reducing nasal/conjunctival vascular engorgement

dosing.maxDose: Not to exceed 3 days continuous use (nasal)

drugs.indications: Nasal congestion, ocular redness, persistent facial erythema of rosacea
drugs.mechanism: Direct alpha-adrenergic agonist producing longer-lasting vasoconstriction than naphazoline; topical form reduces facial vasodilation in rosacea
sideEffects: Rebound congestion with prolonged nasal use

dosing.maxDose: Not to exceed 3 days continuous use

drugs.metabolism: Minimal systemic absorption at recommended doses

drugs.indications: Cardiogenic shock, acute decompensated heart failure, cardiac stress testing
drugs.mechanism: Predominantly beta1 agonist increasing myocardial contractility (positive inotropy) with relatively less chronotropic effect than isoproterenol; also mild beta2/alpha1 activity

drugs.indications: Acute asthma/COPD exacerbation, exercise-induced bronchospasm, hyperkalemia (adjunct)
drugs.mechanism: Selective beta2 agonist causing bronchial smooth muscle relaxation via increased cAMP; also drives potassium intracellularly (used in hyperkalemia)

dosing.maxDose: Every 4-6h PRN, more frequent in acute setting

drugs.clinicalPearls: Overuse (frequent SABA use) is a marker of poor asthma control and increased mortality risk — should not be used as monotherapy for persistent asthma.

drugs.indications: Acute bronchospasm, off-label tocolysis (preterm labor, short-term use)
drugs.mechanism: Selective beta2 agonist relaxing bronchial and uterine smooth muscle
contraindications: Prolonged tocolysis beyond 48-72h (FDA black box warning)

subclass.fr: Sympathomimétique - agoniste bêta2 (longue durée, action rapide)

drugs.indications: Asthma maintenance (always with ICS), COPD maintenance
drugs.mechanism: Highly lipophilic beta2 agonist with rapid onset (~1-3 min, unlike salmeterol) and prolonged duration (~12h) via sustained receptor interaction
sideEffects: Increased asthma-related death if used without ICS (black box)

subclass.fr: Sympathomimétique - agoniste bêta2 (longue durée, action lente)

drugs.indications: Asthma maintenance (with ICS), COPD maintenance
drugs.mechanism: Long side chain anchors to exosite near beta2 receptor allowing prolonged (~12h) receptor engagement; slower onset (~20-30 min) than formoterol, unsuitable for rescue use
sideEffects: Increased asthma mortality without ICS (black box)

drugs.indications: Bradyarrhythmias (temporary), heart block (bridge to pacing), bronchospasm (historical)
drugs.mechanism: Pure beta agonist (beta1 and beta2, no alpha activity) increasing heart rate, contractility, and causing bronchodilation and vasodilation (can drop diastolic BP)

drugs.indications: Overactive bladder (urgency, frequency, urge incontinence)
drugs.mechanism: Selective beta3 agonist relaxing detrusor smooth muscle during bladder filling, increasing bladder capacity without the antimuscarinic side effect profile

drugs.therapeuticClass: Non-selective adrenergic agonist (alpha1, alpha2, beta1, beta2)
drugs.indications: Anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest (ACLS), septic shock (adjunct), local hemostasis (with anesthetics)
drugs.mechanism: Activates all adrenergic receptors: alpha1 (vasoconstriction), beta1 (increased HR/contractility), beta2 (bronchodilation, decreased mediator release) — dose-dependent receptor predominance

dosing.standard: 0.3-0.5 mg IM (anaphylaxis); 1 mg IV every 3-5 min (cardiac arrest)

contraindications: Relative: narrow-angle glaucoma, general anesthesia with halogenated agents (arrhythmia risk) — none absolute in anaphylaxis/cardiac arrest

drugs.indications: Septic shock (first-line vasopressor), other distributive/vasodilatory shock states
drugs.mechanism: Potent alpha1 agonist causing marked vasoconstriction and increased systemic vascular resistance, with modest beta1 activity increasing contractility; minimal beta2 activity

drugs.indications: Hypertension, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), PTSD-associated nightmares (off-label)
drugs.mechanism: Selective alpha1 blockade causing arterial and venous vasodilation, reducing peripheral resistance and blood pressure; relaxes prostatic/bladder neck smooth muscle
drugs.clinicalPearls: Classic 'first-dose phenomenon' — give the first dose at bedtime to avoid syncope from profound first-dose hypotension.

subclass.en: Sympatholytic - selective alpha1 antagonist (with central 5-HT1A action)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Selective alpha1 antagonist with central serotonergic action
drugs.indications: Hypertensive emergencies, perioperative hypertension
drugs.mechanism: Peripheral alpha1 blockade plus central 5-HT1A agonism, lowering blood pressure with less reflex tachycardia than pure alpha blockers

dosing.standard: 25 mg IV bolus, then infusion 9-30 mg/h

drugs.indications: Hypertension, benign prostatic hyperplasia
drugs.mechanism: Long-acting selective alpha1 blockade, longer half-life than prazosin allowing once-daily dosing
sideEffects: Increased heart failure risk (ALLHAT trial finding)

drugs.indications: Benign prostatic hyperplasia, facilitation of ureteral stone passage (off-label)
drugs.mechanism: Selective for alpha1A receptors concentrated in the prostate/bladder neck, relaxing smooth muscle with minimal vascular (alpha1B) effect, reducing hypotension risk vs non-selective alpha1 blockers
drugs.clinicalPearls: Warn cataract surgeons before ophthalmic surgery — associated with intraoperative floppy iris syndrome even after drug discontinuation.

drugs.indications: Pheochromocytoma (perioperative BP control), extravasation of vasopressors (local infiltration), hypertensive crisis from MAOI-tyramine interaction
drugs.mechanism: Competitive, reversible alpha1 and alpha2 blockade causing vasodilation; alpha2 blockade removes negative feedback on norepinephrine release, contributing to reflex tachycardia

dosing.standard: 5 mg IV (pheochromocytoma); 5-10 mg in 10 mL saline infiltrated (extravasation)

drugs.indications: Pheochromocytoma (preoperative preparation, longer-term BP control before surgery)
drugs.mechanism: Irreversible covalent alkylation of alpha1/alpha2 receptors, producing long-lasting blockade that persists until new receptors are synthesized (unlike phentolamine's reversible action)

dosing.standard: 10 mg twice daily, titrate up over 1-2 weeks pre-op

contraindications: Conditions where hypotension would be dangerous (cerebrovascular/coronary disease, relative)

subclass.fr: Sympatholytique - agoniste/antagoniste alpha partiel (alcaloïde de l'ergot)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Ergot alkaloid, partial agonist at alpha-adrenergic and serotonergic (5-HT1) receptors
drugs.indications: Acute migraine and cluster headache (second-line, limited use today)
drugs.mechanism: Partial agonist/antagonist activity at alpha-adrenergic, dopaminergic, and serotonergic receptors causing vasoconstriction of cranial vessels, aborting migraine attacks
contraindications: Concurrent potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (severe ergotism risk)

subclass.fr: Sympatholytique - agoniste/antagoniste alpha partiel (alcaloïde de l'ergot)

drugs.indications: Acute migraine (including status migrainosus), cluster headache
drugs.mechanism: Similar to ergotamine but with less pronounced peripheral vasoconstriction and better tolerability; acts at 5-HT1B/1D and alpha-adrenergic receptors

drugs.indications: Hypertension, angina, migraine prophylaxis, essential tremor, performance anxiety, thyrotoxicosis (adjunct)
drugs.mechanism: Non-selective beta blockade reducing heart rate, contractility, and renin release (beta1) plus bronchoconstriction risk (beta2); highly lipophilic with significant CNS penetration

subclass.fr: Sympatholytique - antagoniste bêta non sélectif (longue durée)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Non-selective beta antagonist, hydrophilic, long half-life
drugs.indications: Hypertension, angina, variceal bleeding prophylaxis in cirrhosis
drugs.mechanism: Non-selective beta1/beta2 blockade; hydrophilic (unlike propranolol) so minimal CNS penetration, allowing once-daily dosing due to long half-life

drugs.indications: Hypertension, angina, post-MI secondary prevention
drugs.mechanism: Selective beta1 blockade at lower doses (selectivity lost at higher doses), reducing heart rate and myocardial oxygen demand; hydrophilic with minimal CNS penetration
drugs.elimination: Renal (primary, unchanged) — requires dose adjustment in renal impairment

drugs.indications: Hypertension, angina, heart failure (succinate ER formulation), post-MI, arrhythmias
drugs.mechanism: Selective beta1 blockade reducing heart rate, contractility, and myocardial oxygen demand; succinate (ER) form specifically evidence-based in HFrEF
sideEffects: Worsening acute decompensated HF if started during decompensation

dosing.standard: 25-100 mg twice daily (tartrate) or 25-200 mg once daily (succinate ER)

drugs.indications: Hypertension, chronic heart failure (HFrEF, evidence-based), angina
drugs.mechanism: Highly beta1-selective blockade with balanced renal/hepatic elimination; one of the three evidence-based beta-blockers in heart failure (with carvedilol, metoprolol succinate)

dosing.standard: 1.25-10 mg once daily (HF, start low and titrate)

subclass.en: Sympatholytic - cardioselective beta1 antagonist with ISA
subclass.fr: Sympatholytique - antagoniste bêta1 cardiosélectif avec ASI

drugs.therapeuticClass: Beta1-selective antagonist with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA)
drugs.indications: Hypertension, ventricular arrhythmias
drugs.mechanism: Beta1-selective blockade with partial agonist activity (ISA), causing less resting bradycardia than pure antagonists while still blunting exercise-induced tachycardia

dosing.standard: 400 mg once daily or 200mg twice daily

subclass.en: Sympatholytic - non-selective beta antagonist with alpha1 blockade (3rd gen)
subclass.fr: Sympatholytique - antagoniste bêta non sélectif avec blocage alpha1 (3e génération)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Combined non-selective beta and alpha1 antagonist
drugs.indications: Chronic heart failure (HFrEF, evidence-based), hypertension, post-MI left ventricular dysfunction
drugs.mechanism: Blocks beta1, beta2, and alpha1 receptors, combining reduced heart rate/contractility with vasodilation; also has antioxidant properties
sideEffects: Worsening HF if started during acute decompensation

dosing.standard: 3.125 mg twice daily initially, titrate slowly (HF)

contraindications: Decompensated (acute) heart failure requiring IV inotropes

subclass.en: Sympatholytic - non-selective beta antagonist with alpha1 blockade (3rd gen)
subclass.fr: Sympatholytique - antagoniste bêta non sélectif avec blocage alpha1 (3e génération)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Combined non-selective beta and alpha1 antagonist
drugs.indications: Hypertensive emergency/urgency, hypertension in pregnancy (preferred agent), pheochromocytoma
drugs.mechanism: Combined alpha1 and non-selective beta blockade (beta effect predominates, ~3-7x stronger than alpha), lowering BP without significant reflex tachycardia

dosing.standard: 20 mg IV bolus, repeat/double every 10 min (hypertensive emergency); 100-400mg oral twice daily
dosing.frequency: IV boluses or infusion; oral 2x daily

drugs.clinicalPearls: First-line IV agent for hypertensive emergencies in pregnancy/eclampsia given its favorable fetal safety profile.

subclass.en: Sympatholytic - cardioselective beta1 antagonist with NO-mediated vasodilation (3rd gen)
subclass.fr: Sympatholytique - antagoniste bêta1 cardiosélectif avec vasodilatation NO-médiée (3e génération)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Highly beta1-selective antagonist with nitric-oxide-mediated vasodilation
drugs.indications: Hypertension
drugs.mechanism: Most beta1-selective agent available, combined with endothelial nitric oxide release causing additional vasodilation, potentially improving hemodynamics and erectile function (compared to older beta-blockers)
sideEffects: Less erectile dysfunction than traditional beta-blockers

drugs.indications: Hypertension (historical, rarely used today)
drugs.mechanism: Irreversibly inhibits VMAT (vesicular monoamine transporter), depleting norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin from presynaptic storage vesicles, reducing sympathetic outflow

dosing.maxDose: 0.25 mg/day (higher doses rarely add benefit, increase toxicity)

drugs.indications: Pheochromocytoma (preoperative preparation, chronic management of inoperable tumors)
drugs.mechanism: Competitively inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis, reducing norepinephrine/epinephrine production at the source

drugs.indications: Hypertension, ADHD (adjunct), opioid/alcohol/nicotine withdrawal symptoms, severe pain (epidural, adjunct)
drugs.mechanism: Stimulates central alpha2 receptors in the brainstem, reducing sympathetic outflow (decreased norepinephrine release), lowering heart rate and blood pressure
sideEffects: Rebound hypertension on abrupt withdrawal (can be severe)
contraindications: None absolute; caution in bradyarrhythmias, severe coronary insufficiency
drugs.clinicalPearls: Never stop abruptly — rebound hypertensive crisis can occur; must be tapered.

drugs.indications: Hypertension in pregnancy (preferred first-line agent, well-established safety record)
drugs.mechanism: Converted to alpha-methylnorepinephrine, a potent central alpha2 agonist reducing sympathetic outflow, similar mechanism to clonidine but via active metabolite
drugs.halfLife: ~1.7 hours (parent, but clinical effect delayed/prolonged due to active metabolite formation)

drugs.indications: Tonic-clonic and partial seizures, status epilepticus
drugs.mechanism: Blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels in their inactivated state, stabilizing neuronal membranes and preventing repetitive high-frequency firing
drugs.metabolism: Hepatic (CYP2C9/2C19, zero-order kinetics at therapeutic doses — saturable)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Zero-order kinetics near therapeutic range means small dose increases can cause disproportionate level increases — narrow therapeutic index requiring level monitoring.

drugs.indications: Partial and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, trigeminal neuralgia, bipolar disorder
drugs.mechanism: Blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels in inactivated state, reducing repetitive neuronal firing; also modulates glutamate release

drugs.therapeuticClass: Voltage-gated sodium channel blocker with glutamate release inhibition
drugs.indications: Partial and generalized seizures, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, bipolar disorder (maintenance)
drugs.mechanism: Blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels reducing glutamate/aspartate release, stabilizing neuronal membranes
sideEffects: Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (dose-titration-dependent — must titrate slowly)
drugs.halfLife: ~25-33 hours (monotherapy); shorter with enzyme inducers, longer with valproate
drugs.clinicalPearls: Must be titrated very slowly over weeks — rapid titration is the single biggest risk factor for life-threatening rash.

drugs.therapeuticClass: Keto-analog of carbamazepine, sodium channel blocker
drugs.indications: Partial seizures (monotherapy or adjunct)
drugs.mechanism: Blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels similar to carbamazepine, converted to active monohydroxy derivative; fewer drug interactions than carbamazepine (weaker enzyme induction)
drugs.metabolism: Hepatic (reduction to active metabolite, not CYP-dependent oxidation like carbamazepine)

subclass.en: Antiepileptic - multiple mechanisms (Na+ channel, GABA, glutamate, carbonic anhydrase)

drugs.indications: Partial and generalized seizures, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, migraine prophylaxis, weight loss (with phentermine)
drugs.mechanism: Blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels, enhances GABA-A activity, blocks AMPA/kainate glutamate receptors, and weakly inhibits carbonic anhydrase — multimodal action

drugs.therapeuticClass: Barbiturate, GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator
drugs.indications: Generalized tonic-clonic and partial seizures, status epilepticus, neonatal seizures
drugs.mechanism: Prolongs GABA-A chloride channel opening duration (distinct from benzodiazepines which increase frequency), causing broad CNS depression at higher doses
drugs.elimination: Renal (25% unchanged, pH-dependent — alkalinization enhances elimination in overdose)

subclass.en: Antiepileptic - GABA-ergic and Na+ channel blocker (broad spectrum)
subclass.fr: Antiépileptique - GABAergique et bloqueur Na+ (large spectre)

drugs.indications: Generalized (absence, myoclonic, tonic-clonic) and partial seizures, bipolar disorder, migraine prophylaxis
drugs.mechanism: Increases GABA levels (inhibits GABA transaminase/increases synthesis), blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels, and inhibits T-type Ca2+ channels — true broad-spectrum action
contraindications: Pregnancy (especially for migraine/bipolar indications — black box)

subclass.fr: Antiépileptique - inhibiteur de la recapture du GABA

drugs.indications: Partial seizures (adjunctive therapy)
drugs.mechanism: Blocks GAT-1 GABA transporter, increasing synaptic GABA concentration and prolonging inhibitory neurotransmission
sideEffects: Non-convulsive status epilepticus (paradoxical, especially off-label use without epilepsy)

drugs.indications: Infantile spasms, refractory complex partial seizures
drugs.mechanism: Irreversibly inhibits GABA transaminase (the enzyme that degrades GABA), increasing GABA concentration in the CNS
sideEffects: Permanent peripheral visual field constriction (black box — requires periodic vision testing)
drugs.halfLife: ~5-8 hours (but pharmacodynamic effect outlasts plasma half-life due to irreversible enzyme inhibition)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Available only through a restricted distribution program (REMS) in the US due to the risk of permanent vision loss.

subclass.fr: Antiépileptique - modulateur des canaux calciques alpha2-delta

drugs.therapeuticClass: Alpha2-delta subunit calcium channel ligand (GABA analog, non-GABAergic mechanism)
drugs.indications: Partial seizures (adjunct), postherpetic neuralgia, neuropathic pain, restless legs syndrome
drugs.mechanism: Binds alpha2-delta subunit of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, reducing calcium influx and neurotransmitter release; despite structural similarity to GABA, does not act on GABA receptors directly
contraindications: None absolute; dose adjustment required in renal impairment

subclass.fr: Antiépileptique - modulateur des canaux calciques alpha2-delta

drugs.therapeuticClass: Alpha2-delta subunit calcium channel ligand (GABA analog)
drugs.indications: Partial seizures (adjunct), neuropathic pain (diabetic, postherpetic, fibromyalgia), generalized anxiety disorder (some countries)
drugs.mechanism: Same mechanism as gabapentin (alpha2-delta calcium channel binding) but with more predictable, linear pharmacokinetics and higher potency
contraindications: None absolute; dose adjustment required in renal impairment

drugs.indications: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, refractory partial seizures (last-line due to toxicity)
drugs.mechanism: Blocks NMDA glutamate receptors and potentiates GABA-A receptor activity — highly effective but severely restricted due to toxicity
drugs.clinicalPearls: Reserved for refractory cases only, with mandatory informed consent and close hematologic/hepatic monitoring due to black box risks.

subclass.fr: Antiépileptique - bloqueur des canaux calciques de type T

drugs.indications: Absence (petit mal) seizures — drug of choice for pure absence epilepsy
drugs.mechanism: Blocks T-type Ca2+ channels in thalamic neurons, interrupting the thalamocortical oscillatory circuit responsible for generating 3 Hz spike-wave discharges characteristic of absence seizures
drugs.clinicalPearls: Not effective against tonic-clonic seizures — if a patient has mixed absence and tonic-clonic seizures, valproate is preferred instead.

drugs.indications: Status epilepticus, seizure prophylaxis when oral phenytoin not feasible
drugs.mechanism: Rapidly converted to phenytoin by phosphatases in blood/tissue; same Na+ channel blocking mechanism, but water-soluble formulation avoids the propylene glycol vehicle toxicity of IV phenytoin

dosing.standard: 15-20 mg PE/kg loading dose (dosed in phenytoin equivalents)

drugs.metabolism: Converted to phenytoin, then hepatic metabolism as phenytoin
drugs.halfLife: ~15 minutes (conversion to phenytoin); phenytoin half-life thereafter (~22h)
contraindications: Sinus bradycardia, heart block (as with phenytoin)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Can be infused faster and given IM (unlike phenytoin) since it lacks the tissue-damaging propylene glycol diluent — 'purple glove syndrome' risk is much lower.

drugs.indications: Partial, myoclonic, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures; increasingly used first-line due to favorable interaction profile
drugs.mechanism: Binds SV2A, a synaptic vesicle glycoprotein involved in neurotransmitter release regulation, modulating (rather than blocking) exocytosis of neurotransmitter-containing vesicles — a mechanism distinct from all other AEDs
sideEffects: Behavioral changes (irritability, aggression — notable and dose-related)
contraindications: None absolute; dose adjustment in renal impairment
drugs.clinicalPearls: Virtually no CYP-mediated drug interactions makes it a favorite for polypharmacy patients — but behavioral/psychiatric side effects are more prominent than most other AEDs.

drugs.indications: Anxiety, status epilepticus, alcohol withdrawal, muscle spasm, procedural sedation
drugs.mechanism: Binds benzodiazepine site on GABA-A receptor, increasing frequency of chloride channel opening, potentiating GABA's inhibitory effect
drugs.halfLife: ~20-100 hours (very long due to active metabolites)

drugs.indications: Anxiety, alcohol withdrawal (first-line for withdrawal protocols)
drugs.mechanism: Same GABA-A potentiation mechanism as other BZDs; first benzodiazepine developed

drugs.indications: Anxiety disorders
drugs.mechanism: Prodrug converted to desmethyldiazepam, the active long-acting metabolite that potentiates GABA-A activity

drugs.indications: Anxiety disorders
drugs.mechanism: Prodrug metabolized to diazepam and desmethyldiazepam, active long-acting GABA-A potentiators

subclass.fr: Benzodiazépine - anxiolytique (courte durée, sans métabolite actif)

drugs.indications: Anxiety, alcohol withdrawal (preferred in hepatic impairment/elderly)
drugs.mechanism: Direct GABA-A potentiation; already the active glucuronidated metabolite of several other BZDs, so requires no hepatic oxidative metabolism
sideEffects: Dependence (lower abuse potential due to slow onset)
drugs.metabolism: Hepatic glucuronidation only (no oxidative/CYP metabolism — 'LOT' drugs safe in liver disease)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Part of the 'LOT' benzodiazepines (Lorazepam, Oxazepam, Temazepam) that undergo only glucuronidation — preferred in patients with liver disease or the elderly.

drugs.indications: Anxiety, alcohol withdrawal, adjunct for partial seizures
drugs.mechanism: Decarboxylated in gastric acid to desmethyldiazepam, the active long-acting metabolite
drugs.metabolism: Gastric conversion + hepatic metabolism of desmethyldiazepam

drugs.indications: Panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder
drugs.mechanism: High-potency GABA-A potentiation with rapid onset; short half-life associated with higher abuse/dependence and interdose rebound anxiety

drugs.indications: Anxiety disorders
drugs.mechanism: Direct GABA-A potentiation, structurally a thienodiazepine (sulfur-containing ring analog)

subclass.fr: Benzodiazépine - anxiolytique (durée intermédiaire, sans métabolite actif)

drugs.indications: Anxiety, status epilepticus (first-line), alcohol withdrawal, procedural sedation, antiemetic (adjunct)
drugs.mechanism: Direct GABA-A potentiation; glucuronidated only (like oxazepam), no oxidative metabolism required
drugs.clinicalPearls: Preferred first-line agent for status epilepticus due to rapid onset and relatively long duration of anticonvulsant effect.

drugs.indications: Anxiety disorders
drugs.mechanism: Direct GABA-A potentiation

drugs.indications: Anxiety, adjunct for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and refractory epilepsy
drugs.mechanism: GABA-A potentiation; the 1,5-benzodiazepine ring structure (vs typical 1,4) is associated with less sedation at equivalent anxiolytic/anticonvulsant doses
drugs.metabolism: Hepatic (CYP3A4, active metabolite norclobazam via CYP2C19)

drugs.indications: Anxiety disorders
drugs.mechanism: Direct GABA-A potentiation; is itself the major active metabolite of diazepam, prazepam, clorazepate, and others

drugs.indications: Anxiety disorders
drugs.mechanism: Prodrug hydrolyzed to active metabolites potentiating GABA-A activity

drugs.indications: Insomnia (short-term), also used for infantile spasms in some countries
drugs.mechanism: GABA-A potentiation promoting sleep onset and maintenance

drugs.indications: Severe insomnia (restricted use in many countries due to abuse potential)
drugs.mechanism: High-potency GABA-A potentiation with strong amnestic effect
sideEffects: Anterograde amnesia (notable, associated with drug-facilitated assault misuse)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Heavily restricted/banned in many countries due to notoriety in drug-facilitated sexual assault ('date rape drug').

subclass.fr: Benzodiazépine - hypnotique (courte durée, sans métabolite actif)

drugs.indications: Insomnia (short-term)
drugs.mechanism: GABA-A potentiation; glucuronidated directly (like lorazepam) without oxidative metabolism
sideEffects: Less next-day hangover than long-acting BZDs

subclass.fr: Benzodiazépine - hypnotique (durée intermédiaire, sans métabolite actif)

drugs.indications: Insomnia (short-term, particularly sleep maintenance)
drugs.mechanism: GABA-A potentiation; part of the 'LOT' glucuronidated-only BZDs, safer in hepatic impairment

drugs.indications: Insomnia (short-term)
drugs.mechanism: GABA-A potentiation, triazolobenzodiazepine structure

drugs.indications: Insomnia (short-term, particularly sleep onset difficulty), jet lag (off-label)
drugs.mechanism: Very short-acting GABA-A potentiation; rapid onset/offset minimizes next-day sedation but is associated with rebound insomnia and amnesia at higher doses
sideEffects: Dependence (high potential due to short action)
contraindications: Concurrent potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (marked interaction risk)

drugs.indications: Insomnia (short-term)
drugs.mechanism: GABA-A potentiation with intermediate duration of action

drugs.indications: Insomnia (sleep onset)
drugs.mechanism: Selectively binds the alpha1 subunit of GABA-A receptors (unlike BZDs which act on multiple alpha subunits), producing predominantly hypnotic rather than anxiolytic/muscle relaxant effects
sideEffects: Complex sleep behaviors (sleepwalking, sleep-driving — black box)

dosing.standard: 5-10 mg at bedtime (women: 5mg due to slower clearance)
dosing.frequency: Once daily at bedtime, immediately before sleep

drugs.clinicalPearls: FDA lowered the recommended dose for women in 2013 due to slower clearance causing next-morning impaired driving even after a full night's sleep.

drugs.indications: Insomnia (sleep onset and maintenance)
drugs.mechanism: Binds GABA-A receptor at a site overlapping the benzodiazepine site, potentiating chloride currents; less alpha-subunit selective than zolpidem
sideEffects: Complex sleep behaviors (less common than zolpidem)

drugs.therapeuticClass: GABA-A modulator and translocator protein (TSPO) ligand
drugs.indications: Anxiety disorders (adjustment disorders with anxiety)
drugs.mechanism: Dual mechanism: direct GABA-A potentiation (different site than BZDs) plus stimulation of TSPO, promoting neurosteroid (allopregnanolone) synthesis
sideEffects: Rash (rare but can be severe — DRESS syndrome reported)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Non-sedating alternative to benzodiazepines for anxiety, without the dependence potential, but carries a rare but serious hypersensitivity/hepatic risk.

drugs.therapeuticClass: First-generation H1 antihistamine with anxiolytic/sedative properties
drugs.indications: Anxiety, pruritus, pre-sedation (anesthesia adjunct)
drugs.mechanism: H1 receptor antagonism producing sedation, plus some anticholinergic and CNS depressant activity contributing to anxiolysis without GABA-A/benzodiazepine site involvement

drugs.indications: Generalized anxiety disorder
drugs.mechanism: Partial agonist at presynaptic and postsynaptic 5-HT1A receptors; no direct GABA-A activity, so lacks sedation, dependence, and withdrawal typical of benzodiazepines — but has delayed onset (2-4 weeks)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Delayed onset of 2-4 weeks means it's ineffective for acute anxiety/panic attacks — not a substitute for BZDs in acute settings, but useful for chronic GAD without dependence risk.

drugs.indications: Allergic rhinitis, urticaria, motion sickness, insomnia (OTC), acute dystonic reactions
drugs.mechanism: Competitive H1 receptor antagonism; crosses blood-brain barrier causing sedation, plus significant anticholinergic and antiemetic (vestibular) activity

drugs.indications: Motion sickness, nausea/vomiting
drugs.mechanism: Salt combination of diphenhydramine and 8-chlorotheophylline; H1 antagonism with anticholinergic action on the vestibular system reducing motion sickness

drugs.therapeuticClass: First-generation H1 antagonist with antidopaminergic activity
drugs.indications: Nausea/vomiting, allergic conditions, sedation (preoperative), motion sickness
drugs.mechanism: H1 antagonism plus D2 dopamine receptor blockade (antiemetic effect at CTZ) and anticholinergic activity; phenothiazine structure
sideEffects: Severe tissue injury/gangrene if IV extravasation (black box)
Respiratory depression in young children (black box, contraindicated <2 years)

drugs.therapeuticClass: First-generation H1 antagonist with sedative/antitussive activity
drugs.indications: Allergic conditions, pruritus, insomnia (children), cough (antitussive)
drugs.mechanism: H1 antagonism with strong sedative and antitussive (central cough suppression) properties, phenothiazine structure

drugs.indications: Allergic rhinitis, common cold symptoms
drugs.mechanism: H1 receptor antagonism; alkylamine class has relatively less sedation than ethanolamines (like diphenhydramine) at equivalent doses

drugs.therapeuticClass: First-generation H1 antagonist (active enantiomer of chlorpheniramine)
drugs.indications: Allergic rhinitis, urticaria, pruritus
drugs.mechanism: H1 antagonism; the dextro-enantiomer, roughly twice as potent as racemic chlorpheniramine, allowing lower doses

drugs.therapeuticClass: First-generation H1 antagonist with serotonin antagonism
drugs.indications: Allergic conditions, appetite stimulation, serotonin syndrome (antidote adjunct), migraine prophylaxis (children)
drugs.mechanism: H1 receptor antagonism plus notable 5-HT2A serotonin receptor antagonism, explaining its use as adjunct treatment in serotonin syndrome and appetite stimulation

drugs.indications: Allergic rhinitis, chronic urticaria
drugs.mechanism: Peripherally-selective H1 antagonism; limited blood-brain barrier penetration reduces sedation compared to 1st generation agents, though it is the most sedating of the 2nd-gen class

drugs.indications: Allergic rhinitis, chronic urticaria
drugs.mechanism: Peripherally-selective H1 antagonism, minimal CNS penetration, essentially non-sedating at standard doses

drugs.indications: Allergic rhinitis, chronic urticaria
drugs.mechanism: Peripherally-selective H1 antagonism, non-sedating; some QT prolongation risk relative to newer 2nd-gen agents

drugs.therapeuticClass: Second-generation H1 antagonist with mast cell stabilizing activity
drugs.indications: Allergic rhinitis, chronic urticaria, allergic asthma (adjunct)
drugs.mechanism: H1 antagonism plus mast cell membrane stabilization reducing mediator release

drugs.therapeuticClass: Third-generation H1 antagonist (active metabolite of terfenadine)
drugs.indications: Allergic rhinitis, chronic urticaria
drugs.mechanism: Active carboxylic acid metabolite of terfenadine; peripherally-selective, minimal CNS penetration, no cardiac QT effects (unlike parent terfenadine which was withdrawn)

dosing.standard: 60 mg twice daily or 180mg once daily

drugs.clinicalPearls: Developed as the safe, non-cardiotoxic active metabolite after terfenadine was withdrawn for QT prolongation/torsades risk.

drugs.therapeuticClass: Third-generation H1 antagonist (active enantiomer of cetirizine)
drugs.indications: Allergic rhinitis, chronic urticaria
drugs.mechanism: Active levo-enantiomer of cetirizine, roughly twice as potent, allowing half the dose
sideEffects: Mild sedation (less than cetirizine but present)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Third-generation H1 antagonist (active metabolite of loratadine)
drugs.indications: Allergic rhinitis, chronic urticaria
drugs.mechanism: Active metabolite of loratadine, peripherally-selective, non-sedating
contraindications: None absolute; caution in significant hepatic/renal impairment

subclass.en: Antihistamine H1 with mast cell stabilizing activity
subclass.fr: Antihistaminique H1 à activité stabilisatrice mastocytaire

drugs.therapeuticClass: H1 antagonist and mast cell stabilizer
drugs.indications: Allergic conjunctivitis, allergic asthma (adjunct, in some countries), allergic rhinitis
drugs.mechanism: Combines H1 receptor antagonism with mast cell membrane stabilization, inhibiting mediator release; some sedation as it crosses BBB

dosing.standard: 1 mg twice daily (oral); 1 drop twice daily (ophthalmic)

drugs.indications: Peptic ulcer disease, GERD, dyspepsia
drugs.mechanism: Competitive H2 receptor antagonism on gastric parietal cells, reducing histamine-stimulated acid secretion
sideEffects: Significant CYP450 inhibition (major drug interaction potential)

dosing.standard: 300 mg 4 times daily or 800mg at bedtime

drugs.metabolism: Hepatic (CYP450 inhibitor — significant interactions with warfarin, phenytoin, theophylline)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Rarely used today due to extensive CYP450 inhibition causing numerous drug interactions and antiandrogenic side effects — largely replaced by other H2 blockers and PPIs.

drugs.indications: Peptic ulcer disease, GERD, dyspepsia (largely withdrawn from many markets)
drugs.mechanism: Competitive H2 receptor antagonism, more potent and fewer drug interactions than cimetidine (minimal CYP450 inhibition)
sideEffects: Withdrawn in many countries (2020) due to NDMA (carcinogen) contamination found in products

drugs.therapeuticClass: H2 receptor antagonist (most potent of the class)
drugs.indications: Peptic ulcer disease, GERD, dyspepsia
drugs.mechanism: Highly potent, selective H2 receptor antagonism; no clinically significant CYP450 interaction, preferred H2 blocker after ranitidine withdrawal

dosing.standard: 20-40 mg twice daily or 40mg at bedtime

contraindications: None absolute; dose adjustment in renal impairment

drugs.indications: Peptic ulcer disease, GERD
drugs.mechanism: Competitive H2 receptor antagonism, minimal hepatic metabolism (mostly renal elimination unchanged)
contraindications: Dose adjustment required in renal impairment

drugs.therapeuticClass: Dopamine precursor (crosses blood-brain barrier, unlike dopamine itself)
drugs.indications: Parkinson's disease (gold standard treatment)
drugs.mechanism: Crosses the blood-brain barrier via the large neutral amino acid transporter, then converted to dopamine by dopa-decarboxylase in surviving nigrostriatal neurons, replenishing depleted striatal dopamine
drugs.metabolism: Peripheral decarboxylation (blocked by carbidopa) and COMT
drugs.halfLife: ~1-3 hours (short, driving motor fluctuations with chronic use)

subclass.fr: Antiparkinsonien - inhibiteur périphérique de la dopa-décarboxylase

drugs.therapeuticClass: Peripheral aromatic amino acid decarboxylase inhibitor
drugs.indications: Always co-administered with levodopa in Parkinson's disease
drugs.mechanism: Does not cross the blood-brain barrier; inhibits peripheral decarboxylation of levodopa to dopamine, increasing the fraction of levodopa reaching the CNS and reducing peripheral side effects (nausea, hypotension)
sideEffects: Contributes to reduced peripheral levodopa side effects
contraindications: None when combined appropriately with levodopa

subclass.fr: Antiparkinsonien - inhibiteur périphérique de la dopa-décarboxylase

drugs.therapeuticClass: Peripheral aromatic amino acid decarboxylase inhibitor
drugs.indications: Always co-administered with levodopa in Parkinson's disease (alternative to carbidopa, used in Europe/other markets)
drugs.mechanism: Same mechanism as carbidopa — peripheral decarboxylase inhibition sparing levodopa for CNS conversion
contraindications: None when combined appropriately with levodopa

subclass.fr: Antiparkinsonien - agoniste dopaminergique direct (dérivé de l'ergot)

drugs.indications: Parkinson's disease (adjunct/monotherapy early disease), hyperprolactinemia, prolactinoma, type 2 diabetes (quick-release formulation)
drugs.mechanism: Direct agonist at D2 dopamine receptors (also some D1 activity), stimulating postsynaptic dopamine receptors independent of presynaptic neuron survival

subclass.fr: Antiparkinsonien - potentialisateur de la libération de dopamine

drugs.therapeuticClass: Dopamine release enhancer and NMDA antagonist
drugs.indications: Parkinson's disease (mild symptoms, or to treat levodopa-induced dyskinesias), influenza A prophylaxis (historical, largely resistant now)
drugs.mechanism: Increases synaptic dopamine release and blocks its reuptake; also NMDA glutamate receptor antagonism contributes to antidyskinetic effect in advanced Parkinson's
drugs.halfLife: ~10-14 hours (much longer in renal impairment — requires dose adjustment)

drugs.indications: Parkinson's disease (early monotherapy or adjunct to levodopa), depression (transdermal, higher doses)
drugs.mechanism: Selectively and irreversibly inhibits MAO-B, the enzyme primarily responsible for dopamine breakdown in the striatum, prolonging dopamine's synaptic action; loses selectivity at higher (antidepressant) doses
contraindications: Doses above 10mg/day with tyramine-restricted diet not needed (selectivity), but required at antidepressant doses

drugs.indications: Parkinson's disease (early monotherapy or adjunct to levodopa)
drugs.mechanism: Selective irreversible MAO-B inhibition, similar to selegiline but not metabolized to amphetamine derivatives, giving a cleaner side-effect profile

drugs.indications: Parkinson's disease adjunct to levodopa/carbidopa (extends 'on' time, reduces wearing-off)
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits peripheral COMT, blocking an alternative metabolic pathway of levodopa, increasing its bioavailability and CNS delivery without crossing the blood-brain barrier itself

dosing.frequency: With each levodopa dose, up to 8-10x/day

contraindications: History of NMS or rhabdomyolysis with dopaminergic drug withdrawal

subclass.fr: Antiparkinsonien - inhibiteur de la COMT (central et périphérique)

drugs.indications: Parkinson's disease adjunct to levodopa (reserved for cases not responding to entacapone, due to hepatotoxicity risk)
drugs.mechanism: Unlike entacapone, crosses the blood-brain barrier providing both central and peripheral COMT inhibition, giving stronger/longer levodopa potentiation but with significant hepatotoxicity risk
sideEffects: Fulminant hepatotoxicity (black box — requires regular LFT monitoring)
contraindications: History of NMS or rhabdomyolysis with dopaminergic drug withdrawal
History of non-traumatic rhabdomyolysis or hyperpyrexia
drugs.clinicalPearls: Requires signed patient consent and regular liver function monitoring due to rare but fatal hepatotoxicity cases — second-line to entacapone.

drugs.indications: Schizophrenia, bipolar disorder (mania/maintenance), treatment-resistant depression (with fluoxetine), chemotherapy-induced nausea (adjunct)
drugs.mechanism: Antagonizes D2 dopaminergic and 5-HT2A serotonergic receptors, with high 5-HT2A:D2 ratio contributing to lower extrapyramidal side effects than typical antipsychotics; also antagonizes H1, muscarinic, and alpha1 receptors
sideEffects: Significant weight gain/metabolic syndrome (notable among atypicals)
Increased mortality in dementia-related psychosis (black box)
contraindications: Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis (black box)

subclass.en: Antipsychotic - atypical (D2/5-HT2A antagonist, weak D2 affinity)
subclass.fr: Antipsychotique - atypique (antagoniste D2/5-HT2A, faible affinité D2)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Second-generation antipsychotic, gold standard for treatment-resistant schizophrenia
drugs.indications: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia, reduction of suicidal behavior in schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder
drugs.mechanism: Relatively weak D2 antagonism (unlike other antipsychotics) combined with strong 5-HT2A, D4, muscarinic, and alpha1 antagonism — thought to explain unique efficacy in refractory cases with minimal extrapyramidal symptoms
sideEffects: Agranulocytosis (black box — requires mandatory REMS blood monitoring)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Requires enrollment in a mandatory monitoring program with regular absolute neutrophil count checks (weekly initially) due to agranulocytosis risk — reserved for treatment-resistant cases only.

drugs.indications: Nausea/vomiting, gastroparesis, gastroesophageal reflux (prokinetic effect)
drugs.mechanism: Blocks D2 receptors at the chemoreceptor trigger zone (which lies outside the blood-brain barrier) and enhances gastric motility; does not readily cross into the CNS, minimizing extrapyramidal side effects
sideEffects: QT prolongation (dose-dependent, black box in some countries)

subclass.en: Antiemetic/prokinetic - central and peripheral D2 antagonist
subclass.fr: Antiémétique/prokinétique - antagoniste D2 central et périphérique

drugs.therapeuticClass: D2 antagonist (central and peripheral) with 5-HT4 agonist/5-HT3 antagonist activity
drugs.indications: Nausea/vomiting (chemotherapy, postoperative), gastroparesis, GERD
drugs.mechanism: Blocks D2 receptors at the CTZ (central antiemetic effect) and in the GI tract, plus 5-HT4 agonism enhancing acetylcholine release for prokinetic effect; crosses the blood-brain barrier (unlike domperidone), explaining its CNS side effects
sideEffects: Extrapyramidal symptoms/tardive dyskinesia (black box with prolonged use — limit to 12 weeks)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Black box warning limits continuous use to 12 weeks due to tardive dyskinesia risk, which can be irreversible.

drugs.therapeuticClass: Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (first ACE inhibitor developed)
drugs.indications: Hypertension, heart failure, post-MI, diabetic nephropathy
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits ACE, blocking conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, reducing vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion; also prevents bradykinin degradation (contributes to cough side effect)
sideEffects: Acute kidney injury (bilateral renal artery stenosis)
Rash/taste disturbance (unique to captopril's sulfhydryl group)

drugs.indications: Hypertension, heart failure
drugs.mechanism: Prodrug hydrolyzed to enalaprilat, the active ACE inhibitor, blocking angiotensin II formation

drugs.indications: Hypertension, heart failure, cardiovascular risk reduction (HOPE trial), diabetic nephropathy
drugs.mechanism: Prodrug converted to active ramiprilat, ACE inhibition blocking angiotensin II formation

drugs.therapeuticClass: ACE inhibitor (already active, no hepatic activation required)
drugs.indications: Hypertension, heart failure, post-MI
drugs.mechanism: Direct ACE inhibition without requiring hepatic conversion (unlike enalapril/ramipril), useful in patients with hepatic impairment

subclass.fr: ARA II (Antagoniste des Récepteurs de l'Angiotensine II)

drugs.indications: Hypertension, diabetic nephropathy, heart failure (ACE-inhibitor intolerant)
drugs.mechanism: Blocks AT1 receptors directly, preventing angiotensin II's vasoconstrictive/aldosterone-stimulating effects without affecting bradykinin metabolism (hence no cough)
sideEffects: Much lower incidence of cough/angioedema than ACE inhibitors

drugs.indications: Hypertension, heart failure, post-MI left ventricular dysfunction
drugs.mechanism: Direct AT1 receptor blockade, no active metabolite required (already active)

drugs.indications: Hypertension, diabetic nephropathy (type 2 diabetes)
drugs.mechanism: Direct AT1 receptor blockade with long half-life allowing once-daily dosing

drugs.therapeuticClass: Direct renin inhibitor (blocks the RAAS cascade at its origin)
drugs.indications: Hypertension (monotherapy, rarely combined with ACEi/ARB due to hyperkalemia/renal risk)
drugs.mechanism: Directly inhibits renin, blocking the conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin I — the earliest point of intervention in the RAAS cascade
drugs.metabolism: Minimal hepatic metabolism (CYP3A4 substrate for the small metabolized fraction)
contraindications: Concurrent ACEi/ARB in diabetic patients (increased renal/hyperkalemia risk — ALTITUDE trial)

subclass.fr: ARNI (Inhibiteur de la Néprilysine et Antagoniste des Récepteurs de l'Angiotensine)

drugs.indications: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) — replaces ACEi/ARB in eligible patients
drugs.mechanism: Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin (the enzyme that degrades natriuretic peptides), increasing beneficial natriuretic peptide levels (vasodilation, natriuresis), while valsartan blocks AT1 receptors — dual RAAS/natriuretic peptide system modulation
sideEffects: Angioedema (must not combine with ACE inhibitor — 36h washout required)

dosing.standard: 49/51 mg twice daily initially, titrate to 97/103mg twice daily

drugs.metabolism: Sacubitril activated by esterases; valsartan minimal metabolism
contraindications: Concurrent or within 36h of ACE inhibitor use (angioedema risk)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Landmark PARADIGM-HF trial showed superiority over enalapril in HFrEF — now guideline-preferred over ACE inhibitors/ARBs alone in eligible heart failure patients.

drugs.indications: Acute migraine attack, cluster headache
drugs.mechanism: Agonizes 5-HT1B receptors causing cranial vasoconstriction and 5-HT1D receptors on trigeminal nerve terminals, inhibiting release of vasoactive neuropeptides (CGRP) — aborts the migraine cascade

dosing.standard: 50-100 mg oral or 6mg SC at onset
dosing.frequency: As needed, may repeat after 2h (oral) or 1h (SC)

drugs.indications: Migraine prophylaxis
drugs.mechanism: Antagonizes 5-HT2 serotonin receptors (thought to reduce migraine frequency through central serotonergic modulation) plus antihistamine and mild anticholinergic activity

dosing.standard: 1.5 mg at bedtime, or divided doses

drugs.indications: Chemotherapy/radiotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, postoperative nausea and vomiting
drugs.mechanism: Blocks 5-HT3 receptors both peripherally (vagal afferents in the GI tract, where chemotherapy triggers serotonin release from enterochromaffin cells) and centrally at the chemoreceptor trigger zone
sideEffects: Serotonin syndrome risk (with other serotonergic drugs)

dosing.maxDose: 32 mg/day (single-day IV limit due to QT risk)

drugs.indications: Major depressive disorder, social anxiety disorder
drugs.mechanism: Reversibly and selectively inhibits MAO-A, increasing synaptic serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine; reversibility reduces the tyramine ('cheese') reaction risk compared to older irreversible MAOIs
sideEffects: Lower tyramine reaction risk than classic MAOIs but dietary caution still advised at high doses

drugs.indications: Major depressive disorder, OCD, bulimia nervosa, panic disorder, PMDD
drugs.mechanism: Selectively inhibits presynaptic serotonin reuptake transporter (SERT), increasing synaptic serotonin availability
drugs.halfLife: ~1-6 days (parent); 4-16 days (norfluoxetine — longest of all SSRIs)
contraindications: Concurrent MAOI use (within 14 days; 5 weeks washout after stopping fluoxetine given long half-life)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Longest half-life of any SSRI (due to active metabolite) — lowest discontinuation syndrome risk but longest washout period needed before starting an MAOI.

drugs.indications: Major depressive disorder
drugs.mechanism: Selective SERT inhibition, one of the most selective SSRIs (minimal off-target receptor activity)
sideEffects: QT prolongation (dose-dependent — FDA dose cap warning)

dosing.maxDose: 40 mg/day (20mg if >60 years or hepatic impairment, due to QT risk)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (active enantiomer of citalopram)
drugs.indications: Major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder
drugs.mechanism: Active S-enantiomer of citalopram, roughly twice as potent, with the R-enantiomer removed (which was pharmacologically inactive/potentially antagonistic to the S-form's effect)
sideEffects: QT prolongation (less pronounced than citalopram but present)

drugs.indications: OCD, social anxiety disorder, major depressive disorder
drugs.mechanism: Selective SERT inhibition; notable for potent CYP1A2 inhibition causing significant drug interactions (e.g., with theophylline, clozapine, caffeine)
drugs.metabolism: Hepatic (CYP1A2, 2D6 — also a potent CYP1A2 inhibitor itself)

drugs.indications: Major depressive disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety, GAD, PTSD
drugs.mechanism: Potent SERT inhibition, also has mild anticholinergic and norepinephrine reuptake inhibition properties at higher doses
sideEffects: Highest anticholinergic burden of the SSRIs (dry mouth, constipation)
drugs.metabolism: Hepatic (CYP2D6, potent inhibitor of its own metabolism — nonlinear kinetics)
contraindications: Pregnancy (category concerns re: cardiac malformations, particularly 1st trimester)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Shortest half-life among SSRIs combined with potent self-inhibition of metabolism gives it the most pronounced discontinuation syndrome — taper carefully.

drugs.indications: Major depressive disorder, panic disorder, OCD, PTSD, social anxiety, PMDD
drugs.mechanism: Selective SERT inhibition with mild dopamine reuptake inhibition (weakest of the class, of debated clinical significance)
sideEffects: GI upset (notably diarrhea, more than other SSRIs)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Considered among the safer SSRIs in pregnancy and in patients with cardiac disease due to a favorable drug interaction profile — often a first-line choice.

drugs.indications: Major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety
drugs.mechanism: Dose-dependent dual reuptake inhibition — predominantly serotonergic at low doses, with increasing norepinephrine reuptake inhibition at higher doses

drugs.indications: Major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, fibromyalgia, chronic musculoskeletal pain
drugs.mechanism: Balanced dual serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibition at all doses (unlike venlafaxine's dose-dependent shift)

drugs.indications: Major depressive disorder, nocturnal enuresis (children), panic disorder
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits reuptake of both serotonin and norepinephrine (less selectively than SNRIs), plus significant antihistamine, anticholinergic, and alpha1-adrenergic blocking activity accounting for its extensive side-effect profile
sideEffects: Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Highly lethal in overdose due to cardiotoxicity (QRS widening, arrhythmias) — largely superseded by SSRIs/SNRIs as first-line given the much wider safety margin of newer agents.

drugs.indications: Adrenal insufficiency (replacement), inflammatory conditions, anaphylaxis (adjunct), septic shock (stress dose)
drugs.mechanism: Binds intracellular glucocorticoid receptors, translocating to the nucleus to modulate gene transcription — inhibits phospholipase A2 (reducing arachidonic acid/prostaglandin synthesis) and suppresses pro-inflammatory cytokines

drugs.indications: Wide range of inflammatory/autoimmune conditions (asthma, rheumatoid arthritis, IBD, transplant rejection prophylaxis)
drugs.mechanism: Prodrug converted to active prednisolone by hepatic 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase; glucocorticoid receptor-mediated anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressive gene transcription effects
contraindications: Significant hepatic impairment (conversion impaired — use prednisolone directly instead)

subclass.fr: Corticostéroïde - synthétique non halogéné (non compensé, forme active)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Synthetic glucocorticoid (already active, no hepatic conversion needed)
drugs.indications: Same as prednisone; preferred in hepatic impairment
drugs.mechanism: Direct glucocorticoid receptor agonist, same downstream anti-inflammatory transcriptional effects as prednisone without requiring hepatic activation

drugs.therapeuticClass: Synthetic glucocorticoid, higher anti-inflammatory potency, minimal mineralocorticoid activity
drugs.indications: Acute exacerbations (COPD, MS), severe allergic reactions, pulse therapy for autoimmune conditions
drugs.mechanism: Same glucocorticoid receptor mechanism, with the methyl group reducing mineralocorticoid (sodium/water retention) activity compared to hydrocortisone/prednisone
sideEffects: Fewer fluid retention effects than hydrocortisone

dosing.standard: 4-48 mg/day oral; 1g IV daily for 3-5 days (pulse therapy)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Synthetic glucocorticoid with minimal mineralocorticoid activity
drugs.indications: Intra-articular injection (osteoarthritis/inflammatory arthritis), dermatologic conditions (topical), allergic rhinitis (intranasal)
drugs.mechanism: Glucocorticoid receptor agonist with negligible mineralocorticoid effect, useful for local/depot administration

dosing.frequency: Not more than every 3 months per joint

drugs.halfLife: ~2-5 hours (depot formulations provide prolonged local effect)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Highly potent, long-acting synthetic glucocorticoid, no mineralocorticoid activity
drugs.indications: Cerebral edema, COVID-19 (severe, requiring oxygen), antenatal fetal lung maturation, chemotherapy-induced nausea (adjunct), croup
drugs.mechanism: Very high glucocorticoid receptor affinity/potency (~25-30x hydrocortisone) with essentially zero mineralocorticoid activity and long duration of action

drugs.therapeuticClass: Highly potent, long-acting synthetic glucocorticoid (stereoisomer of dexamethasone)
drugs.indications: Antenatal fetal lung maturation (preterm labor), dermatologic conditions (topical), inflammatory conditions
drugs.mechanism: Same high-potency glucocorticoid receptor mechanism as dexamethasone with negligible mineralocorticoid activity
sideEffects: Neonatal effects if repeated antenatal courses

dosing.standard: 12 mg IM x2 doses 24h apart (fetal lung maturation)

drugs.indications: Pain, fever, inflammation, cardiovascular event prophylaxis (antiplatelet, low-dose)
drugs.mechanism: Irreversibly acetylates COX-1 and COX-2, blocking prostaglandin/thromboxane synthesis; at low doses, selectively suppresses platelet thromboxane A2 (antiplatelet effect lasts the platelet's ~10-day lifespan since platelets lack nuclei to resynthesize COX)
sideEffects: Reye's syndrome (children with viral illness — avoid)
drugs.metabolism: Hepatic (esterase hydrolysis to salicylic acid, then conjugation)
drugs.elimination: Renal (dose-dependent kinetics — zero-order at high/toxic doses)
drugs.halfLife: ~15-20 min (aspirin); ~2-3h (salicylate, low dose); up to 20h (high dose, saturated metabolism)

drugs.indications: Gout (acute), ankylosing spondylitis, patent ductus arteriosus closure (neonates)
drugs.mechanism: Reversible, competitive nonselective COX inhibition, one of the most potent NSAIDs; in neonates, closes the PDA by inhibiting prostaglandin E2 (which normally keeps the ductus patent)

drugs.indications: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis
drugs.mechanism: Nonselective COX inhibition; very long half-life allows once-daily dosing
sideEffects: GI ulceration (higher risk than other NSAIDs, given long half-life/exposure)

drugs.indications: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis
drugs.mechanism: Relative COX-2 selectivity at lower doses (theoretically less GI toxicity than nonselective NSAIDs, though selectivity is only partial and dose-dependent)
sideEffects: GI ulceration (lower than nonselective NSAIDs but not absent)

drugs.indications: Pain, fever, inflammation (mild-moderate, most widely used OTC NSAID)
drugs.mechanism: Reversible, competitive nonselective COX inhibition, generally favorable safety/efficacy balance among NSAIDs
sideEffects: GI ulceration (lower risk than aspirin/indomethacin at standard doses)
May reduce aspirin's antiplatelet effect if taken concurrently

drugs.indications: Pain, inflammation (musculoskeletal, dysmenorrhea)
drugs.mechanism: Nonselective COX inhibition, also weak lipoxygenase inhibition

subclass.fr: AINS - dérivé de l'acide propionique (longue durée)

drugs.indications: Pain, inflammation, considered among lower cardiovascular-risk NSAIDs
drugs.mechanism: Nonselective COX inhibition; longer half-life allows twice-daily dosing; epidemiologic data suggest relatively lower cardiovascular risk compared to other NSAIDs
sideEffects: Lower cardiovascular risk relative to some other NSAIDs (but not zero)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Nonselective COX inhibitor with relative COX-2 preference
drugs.indications: Pain, inflammation (osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, acute musculoskeletal pain)
drugs.mechanism: Nonselective COX inhibition with somewhat greater COX-2 relative potency than other traditional NSAIDs
sideEffects: Hepatotoxicity (higher relative risk than other NSAIDs)
Cardiovascular risk (relatively higher among NSAIDs per some meta-analyses)

subclass.fr: AINS - inhibiteur sélectif de la COX-2 (coxib)

drugs.indications: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, acute pain — designed to reduce GI toxicity vs nonselective NSAIDs
drugs.mechanism: Selectively inhibits COX-2 (inducible, inflammation-associated) while sparing COX-1 (constitutive, gastroprotective), reducing GI ulceration risk relative to nonselective NSAIDs while retaining anti-inflammatory efficacy
sideEffects: Cardiovascular risk (class concern, though comparable to some nonselective NSAIDs at matched doses per PRECISION trial)
Lower GI toxicity than nonselective NSAIDs

subclass.fr: AINS - inhibiteur sélectif de la COX-2 (coxib, retiré)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Selective COX-2 inhibitor (historical — withdrawn from market)
drugs.indications: Formerly: osteoarthritis, acute pain (withdrawn worldwide in 2004)
drugs.mechanism: Highly selective COX-2 inhibition without any COX-1 activity, more selective than celecoxib
sideEffects: Significantly increased myocardial infarction/stroke risk (VIGOR trial finding — led to voluntary market withdrawal)
contraindications: No longer marketed — historical/exam reference for COX-2 cardiovascular risk case study
drugs.clinicalPearls: Landmark case in pharmacovigilance history — its 2004 withdrawal reshaped how the FDA/EMA approach cardiovascular risk signals for chronic-use drugs.

drugs.therapeuticClass: Nonselective COX inhibitor (older generation, restricted use)
drugs.indications: Ankylosing spondylitis (severe, refractory cases — restricted due to toxicity), veterinary use (common)
drugs.mechanism: Nonselective COX inhibition, historically one of the first NSAIDs but with a much higher toxicity profile than modern agents
sideEffects: Aplastic anemia/agranulocytosis (significant risk, main reason for restricted human use)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Withdrawn or heavily restricted for human use in most countries due to bone marrow toxicity — mostly encountered today in veterinary medicine.

drugs.indications: Pain, inflammation (musculoskeletal), ENT infections (adjunct anti-inflammatory, in some countries)
drugs.mechanism: Nonselective COX inhibition; fenamates also have some direct prostaglandin receptor antagonist activity

drugs.therapeuticClass: Central COX inhibitor (weak peripheral anti-inflammatory activity)
drugs.indications: Pain, fever — first-line analgesic/antipyretic given favorable safety profile
drugs.mechanism: Mechanism not fully elucidated; thought to inhibit central COX (possibly a COX-3 variant) and involve the endocannabinoid/serotonergic systems; minimal peripheral COX inhibition explains lack of anti-inflammatory and antiplatelet effects (unlike NSAIDs)
sideEffects: Hepatotoxicity (dose-dependent, black box in combination products — leading cause of acute liver failure in overdose)

dosing.maxDose: 4000 mg/day (3000mg/day often recommended for chronic use/at-risk patients)

drugs.metabolism: Hepatic (glucuronidation/sulfation primarily; minor CYP2E1 pathway produces toxic NAPQI metabolite, normally detoxified by glutathione)
contraindications: Chronic alcohol use (increased hepatotoxicity risk via CYP2E1 induction/glutathione depletion)
drugs.clinicalPearls: N-acetylcysteine is the antidote for overdose, working by replenishing glutathione stores to detoxify the NAPQI metabolite before it causes hepatocellular necrosis.

drugs.indications: Moderate-severe pain, fever refractory to other antipyretics (banned in several countries including US, UK due to agranulocytosis risk)
drugs.mechanism: Weak peripheral COX inhibition plus central mechanisms (possibly involving cannabinoid and opioidergic systems); potent analgesic/antipyretic effect disproportionate to its weak COX activity
sideEffects: Agranulocytosis (rare but potentially fatal — main reason for restriction/ban in many countries)
contraindications: Not approved in US, UK, several other countries

drugs.indications: NSAID-induced peptic ulcer prevention, medical abortion (with mifepristone), labor induction, postpartum hemorrhage
drugs.mechanism: Mimics endogenous PGE1, stimulating gastric mucus/bicarbonate secretion and reducing acid secretion (gastroprotective use); also stimulates uterine contraction and cervical ripening (obstetric use)
sideEffects: Uterine contractions/miscarriage risk (contraindicated in pregnancy unless intended)
contraindications: Pregnancy (unless indication is pregnancy termination/labor induction — otherwise absolute contraindication given abortifacient risk)

drugs.indications: Erectile dysfunction (intracavernosal/intraurethral), maintaining ductus arteriosus patency in ductal-dependent congenital heart disease (neonates)
drugs.mechanism: PGE1 receptor agonism causing smooth muscle relaxation — vasodilation of corpus cavernosum arterioles (erection) or maintenance of ductus arteriosus patency in neonates awaiting surgical correction of duct-dependent cardiac lesions
sideEffects: Apnea (neonatal IV use — requires respiratory monitoring)
drugs.metabolism: Rapid pulmonary/hepatic metabolism (extensive first-pass in lungs)
contraindications: Conditions predisposing to priapism (sickle cell, leukemia)

drugs.indications: Cervical ripening and labor induction, second-trimester pregnancy termination
drugs.mechanism: PGE2 receptor agonism causing cervical ripening (collagen breakdown/softening) and uterine smooth muscle contraction

dosing.standard: 10 mg vaginal insert (controlled release) or 0.5mg gel
dosing.frequency: Single insert (12h) or repeat gel doses per protocol

contraindications: Six or more prior term pregnancies

drugs.indications: Pulmonary arterial hypertension, severe Raynaud's phenomenon/critical limb ischemia
drugs.mechanism: PGI2 receptor agonism causing pulmonary and systemic vasodilation, plus inhibition of platelet aggregation

dosing.frequency: 6-9 times daily (inhaled, short duration of action)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Synthetic prostacyclin (PGI2), first agent of this class
drugs.indications: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (severe, WHO functional class III-IV)
drugs.mechanism: PGI2 receptor agonism causing potent pulmonary/systemic vasodilation and platelet aggregation inhibition; extremely short half-life requires continuous infusion via indwelling catheter
sideEffects: Catheter-related bloodstream infection (major risk given permanent line)
Rebound pulmonary hypertension if infusion interrupted (can be fatal)
contraindications: Chronic heart failure with severely reduced LVEF (pulmonary edema risk)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Interruption of the infusion (pump failure, line issues) can cause rapid, life-threatening rebound pulmonary hypertension — patients must never be without backup infusion supplies.

drugs.therapeuticClass: Synthetic prostacyclin (PGI2) analog with greater chemical stability
drugs.indications: Pulmonary arterial hypertension
drugs.mechanism: Same PGI2 receptor agonism as epoprostenol, but chemically stable at room temperature with a much longer half-life, allowing subcutaneous administration and less frequent dosing

drugs.indications: Hypertension, angina, Raynaud's phenomenon
drugs.mechanism: Blocks L-type Ca2+ channels predominantly in vascular smooth muscle (minimal cardiac effect), causing arterial vasodilation and reduced peripheral resistance

dosing.frequency: Once daily (ER only — IR formulation avoided due to reflex tachycardia/MI risk)

contraindications: Immediate-release form in acute coronary syndrome/hypertensive urgency (reflex tachycardia risk)

drugs.indications: Hypertensive emergency, angina
drugs.mechanism: Vascular-selective L-type Ca2+ channel blockade, IV form allows rapid, titratable BP control

drugs.therapeuticClass: L-type calcium channel blocker, long half-life
drugs.indications: Hypertension, chronic stable angina, vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina
drugs.mechanism: Vascular-selective L-type Ca2+ channel blockade; very long half-life gives smooth, sustained BP control without the reflex tachycardia seen with immediate-release nifedipine

drugs.therapeuticClass: L-type calcium channel blocker, high lipophilicity/CNS penetration
drugs.indications: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (prevention of cerebral vasospasm — specific, dedicated indication)
drugs.mechanism: Highly lipophilic, crosses the blood-brain barrier preferentially to act on cerebral vasculature, reducing vasospasm-related ischemic complications after subarachnoid hemorrhage — does NOT primarily treat systemic hypertension despite being a CCB
drugs.clinicalPearls: Improves neurological outcomes after subarachnoid hemorrhage without significantly changing angiographic vasospasm — the mechanism of clinical benefit is thought to be neuroprotective rather than purely vasodilatory.

drugs.indications: Hypertension
drugs.mechanism: Vascular-selective L-type Ca2+ channel blockade with high vascular:cardiac selectivity ratio
drugs.metabolism: Hepatic (CYP3A4 — notable grapefruit juice interaction, significantly increases levels)

drugs.therapeuticClass: L-type calcium channel blocker with combined cardiac and vascular effects
drugs.indications: Hypertension, angina, atrial fibrillation/flutter (rate control), SVT
drugs.mechanism: Blocks L-type Ca2+ channels in both vascular smooth muscle and cardiac tissue (SA/AV nodes), causing vasodilation plus negative chronotropic/dromotropic effects — intermediate between dihydropyridines and verapamil

dosing.frequency: Once daily (ER) or IV bolus/infusion (acute rate control)

contraindications: Sick sinus syndrome/2nd-3rd degree AV block (without pacemaker)
Decompensated heart failure with reduced EF

drugs.therapeuticClass: L-type calcium channel blocker with the strongest cardiac (negative inotropic/chronotropic) effect of the class
drugs.indications: Hypertension, angina, SVT (including acute termination), atrial fibrillation/flutter (rate control), migraine prophylaxis (cluster headache)
drugs.mechanism: Most cardioselective of the non-dihydropyridine CCBs, strongly slows AV nodal conduction (useful for terminating reentrant SVT) and reduces myocardial contractility, with less vascular selectivity than diltiazem
sideEffects: Negative inotropy (caution in heart failure with reduced EF)

dosing.standard: 80-120 mg 3 times daily (IR) or 180-480mg once daily (ER)

contraindications: Sick sinus syndrome/2nd-3rd degree AV block
Decompensated heart failure with reduced EF
Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome with atrial fibrillation (can accelerate conduction via accessory pathway)

drugs.therapeuticClass: ATP-sensitive K+ channel opener (also covered under Nitric Oxide domain — dual mechanism)
drugs.indications: Angina prophylaxis and treatment
drugs.mechanism: Opens ATP-sensitive K+ channels causing arterial vasodilation and mimicking ischemic preconditioning, combined with a nitrate moiety

drugs.therapeuticClass: ATP-sensitive K+ channel opener (potent direct arterial vasodilator)
drugs.indications: Severe/resistant hypertension (oral), androgenetic alopecia (topical)
drugs.mechanism: Opens ATP-sensitive K+ channels in vascular smooth muscle causing hyperpolarization and potent arterial (not venous) vasodilation; topical form's hair growth effect is a separate, incompletely understood mechanism
contraindications: Must be co-administered with a beta-blocker and diuretic in most cases (oral use)

drugs.indications: Hypertension (particularly in pregnancy/preeclampsia), hypertensive emergency
drugs.mechanism: Direct arteriolar smooth muscle relaxation via mechanisms including nitric oxide release and possibly K+ channel involvement, reducing peripheral vascular resistance
contraindications: Severe coronary artery disease (reflex tachycardia risk)

subclass.en: Potassium channel activator - insulin secretion inhibitor
subclass.fr: Activateur des canaux potassiques - inhibiteur de la sécrétion d'insuline

drugs.therapeuticClass: ATP-sensitive K+ channel opener (pancreatic beta-cell selective at therapeutic doses)
drugs.indications: Hypoglycemia due to hyperinsulinism (insulinoma, congenital hyperinsulinism) — NOT primarily used for hypertension despite vasodilator activity
drugs.mechanism: Opens ATP-sensitive K+ channels on pancreatic beta cells, hyperpolarizing the membrane and suppressing insulin release (opposite mechanism/effect of sulfonylureas, which close these same channels)
sideEffects: Hyperglycemia (intended effect but can be excessive)

subclass.fr: Bloqueur des canaux potassiques - sulfamide hypoglycémiant

drugs.therapeuticClass: ATP-sensitive K+ channel blocker (pancreatic beta-cell), insulin secretagogue
drugs.indications: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
drugs.mechanism: Blocks ATP-sensitive K+ channels on pancreatic beta cells, causing membrane depolarization, Ca2+ influx, and insulin release — opposite mechanism to diazoxide

subclass.fr: Bloqueur des canaux potassiques - sulfamide hypoglycémiant

drugs.therapeuticClass: ATP-sensitive K+ channel blocker, insulin secretagogue
drugs.indications: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
drugs.mechanism: Same ATP-sensitive K+ channel blockade mechanism as glibenclamide; considered to have somewhat lower hypoglycemia risk and possibly beneficial antioxidant properties

dosing.standard: 40-80 mg once daily (or 30-120mg MR once daily)

drugs.therapeuticClass: ATP-sensitive K+ channel blocker (rapid, short-acting insulin secretagogue)
drugs.indications: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (particularly for postprandial glucose control)
drugs.mechanism: Same ATP-sensitive K+ channel blockade as sulfonylureas but binds a different site with much faster onset/offset, taken with meals to target postprandial glucose excursions specifically
sideEffects: Hypoglycemia (lower risk than sulfonylureas due to short action)
Must be skipped if meal is skipped (dosing flexibility)

subclass.fr: Antiarythmique - Classe III (bloqueur des canaux potassiques)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Class III antiarrhythmic (also has Class I, II, IV activity — broad-spectrum)
drugs.indications: Ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation, atrial fibrillation (rhythm/rate control), cardiac arrest (ACLS)
drugs.mechanism: Primarily blocks K+ channels (prolonging repolarization/action potential duration and QT interval), but also has Na+ channel blocking (Class I), beta-blocking (Class II), and Ca2+ channel blocking (Class IV) properties — most broad-spectrum antiarrhythmic
sideEffects: QT prolongation/torsades (paradoxically lower risk than other Class III agents)
contraindications: Severe sinus node dysfunction/AV block (without pacemaker)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Its extraordinarily long half-life (weeks to months) means loading doses are required for efficacy, and side effects/interactions can persist long after discontinuation.

subclass.en: Antiarrhythmic - Class III (potassium channel blocker) with beta-blocking activity
subclass.fr: Antiarythmique - Classe III (bloqueur des canaux potassiques) avec activité bêtabloquante

drugs.therapeuticClass: Class III antiarrhythmic combined with non-selective beta-blockade (Class II)
drugs.indications: Ventricular arrhythmias, atrial fibrillation (rhythm control)
drugs.mechanism: Blocks K+ channels (prolonging repolarization, Class III) combined with non-selective beta-adrenergic blockade (Class II) — the two activities work synergistically for rhythm control but combine to increase torsades risk
sideEffects: QT prolongation/torsades de pointes (significant, dose-dependent — requires ECG monitoring at initiation)

dosing.standard: 80 mg twice daily, titrate under monitoring

drugs.clinicalPearls: Initiation typically requires inpatient ECG monitoring given the dose-dependent torsades risk, especially at higher doses or in patients with renal impairment (which prolongs elimination and increases QT effect).

drugs.indications: Adjunct to general anesthesia, procedural analgesia/sedation, labor analgesia
