drugs.mechanism: Weak anesthetic (low potency, high MAC) acting partly via NMDA receptor antagonism; used mainly as an adjunct to reduce requirements of more potent volatile agents and for its analgesic properties
sideEffects: Diffusion hypoxia (rapid emergence, must give 100% O2 after)
Vitamin B12 inactivation (prolonged/repeated exposure — subacute combined degeneration risk)
Expansion of closed air spaces (pneumothorax risk)

drugs.indications: General anesthesia (largely replaced by newer agents in most developed countries)
drugs.mechanism: Potentiates GABA-A and glycine receptors while inhibiting excitatory NMDA/nicotinic receptors, producing dose-dependent CNS depression; high potency (low MAC)
sideEffects: Halothane hepatitis (rare but potentially fatal immune-mediated hepatotoxicity — main reason for decline in use)
drugs.metabolism: Hepatic (~20%, oxidative — produces reactive metabolites implicated in hepatotoxicity)
contraindications: Unexplained fever/jaundice after prior halothane exposure

drugs.indications: General anesthesia maintenance
drugs.mechanism: Same GABA-A potentiation/NMDA inhibition mechanism, minimal cardiac sensitization to catecholamines (safer than halothane in this regard), less hepatotoxic
sideEffects: Airway irritation (pungent odor, less suitable for inhalational induction)

drugs.indications: General anesthesia induction (especially pediatric — mask induction) and maintenance
drugs.mechanism: GABA-A potentiation mechanism; non-pungent odor and rapid onset/offset (low blood-gas solubility) make it ideal for smooth mask induction, particularly in children
sideEffects: Compound A formation with low-flow circuits/soda lime (theoretical nephrotoxicity, rarely clinically significant)
drugs.halfLife: N/A (very rapid pulmonary elimination due to low blood-gas solubility)
drugs.clinicalPearls: The agent of choice for inhalational induction in children due to its pleasant smell and rapid, smooth onset — unlike the pungent, airway-irritating isoflurane/desflurane.

subclass.fr: Anesthésique inhalé - volatil halogéné (action la plus rapide)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Volatile halogenated general anesthetic, lowest blood-gas solubility of modern agents
drugs.indications: General anesthesia maintenance, especially for rapid emergence (day surgery, obese patients)
drugs.mechanism: Same GABA-A mechanism; the lowest blood-gas solubility of the volatile agents gives the fastest onset and (especially) fastest emergence, useful for outpatient surgery
sideEffects: Airway irritation (pungent, unsuitable for induction — coughing/laryngospasm)
Tachycardia/hypertension (sympathetic stimulation with rapid concentration increases)
Higher environmental global warming potential (notable sustainability concern)
drugs.metabolism: Minimal hepatic metabolism (~0.02%, least of all volatile agents)
drugs.halfLife: N/A (fastest pulmonary elimination of volatile agents)
contraindications: Not used for inhalational induction (airway irritation)

drugs.indications: Rapid sequence induction of general anesthesia (historical — largely replaced by propofol), status epilepticus (refractory), medically induced coma (elevated ICP)
drugs.mechanism: Potentiates GABA-A receptor chloride currents (prolongs channel opening), producing rapid unconsciousness; redistribution from brain to peripheral tissues (not metabolism) accounts for rapid awakening after a single dose
sideEffects: Laryngospasm (less airway-protective reflexes preserved than propofol)
drugs.metabolism: Hepatic (slow, CYP-mediated — accumulates with repeated dosing)
drugs.halfLife: ~10-12 hours (context-sensitive half-life increases markedly with repeated/prolonged dosing due to slow hepatic clearance despite fast single-dose redistribution)

drugs.therapeuticClass: IV general anesthetic/sedative-hypnotic (most widely used IV induction agent today)
drugs.indications: Induction and maintenance of general anesthesia, procedural sedation, ICU sedation
drugs.mechanism: Potentiates GABA-A receptor activity, producing rapid onset (one arm-brain circulation time) and rapid, clear-headed emergence due to fast redistribution and hepatic clearance; also has antiemetic properties
sideEffects: Hypotension (significant, from vasodilation and myocardial depression)
Injection pain (common, mitigated by lidocaine co-administration)
Propofol infusion syndrome (rare but fatal — prolonged high-dose infusion, especially in critically ill/pediatric patients)
drugs.halfLife: ~1.5-12 hours (context-sensitive, but rapid clinical recovery due to redistribution)
contraindications: Egg/soy allergy (formulation contains egg lecithin/soybean oil — relative, debated)
Severe hemodynamic instability (relative, caution with hypotension)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Propofol infusion syndrome (rhabdomyolysis, metabolic acidosis, cardiac failure) is a rare but life-threatening complication of prolonged high-dose infusions — most reported in ICU sedation, not brief anesthesia.

drugs.therapeuticClass: IV induction agent with minimal hemodynamic effect
drugs.indications: Induction of general anesthesia, particularly in hemodynamically unstable patients (trauma, cardiac disease)
drugs.mechanism: Potentiates GABA-A receptor activity; notable for minimal effect on blood pressure/cardiac output compared to propofol or thiopental, making it preferred in unstable patients
sideEffects: Adrenal suppression (inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase, even after single dose — significant concern in septic/critically ill patients)

dosing.maxDose: Single induction dose only (not for infusion given adrenal suppression)

drugs.halfLife: ~2.9-5.3 hours (but clinical effect brief due to redistribution)
contraindications: Sepsis (relative — adrenal suppression concern debated but generally avoided or mitigated with stress-dose steroids)

drugs.indications: Induction/maintenance of anesthesia (especially trauma, hemodynamically unstable, bronchospasm/asthma), procedural sedation, analgesia, treatment-resistant depression (sub-anesthetic doses)
drugs.mechanism: Non-competitive NMDA glutamate receptor antagonist, producing a dissociative state (functional/electrophysiological disconnect between cortical and limbic systems) rather than classic GABA-ergic unconsciousness; also has some opioid receptor and monoamine reuptake inhibition activity, and bronchodilator properties
sideEffects: Emergence delirium/hallucinations (notable, can be mitigated with benzodiazepine co-administration)
contraindications: Significant coronary artery disease (increases myocardial oxygen demand)
Increased intracranial pressure (historically avoided, though evidence for this is now debated)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Unique among anesthetics for preserving airway reflexes and respiratory drive while producing profound analgesia — a favorite in prehospital/battlefield medicine and pediatric procedural sedation.

drugs.therapeuticClass: Selective alpha2-adrenergic agonist (central), sedative without significant respiratory depression
drugs.indications: ICU sedation, procedural sedation, adjunct to general anesthesia (reduces opioid/anesthetic requirements)
drugs.mechanism: Agonizes central alpha2 receptors in the locus coeruleus, producing a sedative state resembling natural sleep with preserved arousability and minimal respiratory depression (unlike GABA-ergic sedatives)

dosing.standard: 1 mcg/kg loading over 10 min, then 0.2-0.7 mcg/kg/h infusion

drugs.therapeuticClass: Short-acting benzodiazepine used for anesthesia premedication/induction
drugs.indications: Preoperative anxiolysis/amnesia, procedural sedation, co-induction agent for general anesthesia
drugs.mechanism: GABA-A receptor potentiation (same as other BZDs); water-soluble at low pH, becomes lipid-soluble at physiological pH allowing rapid CNS penetration and short duration
drugs.clinicalPearls: Reversal available with flumazenil (benzodiazepine antagonist) — important for over-sedation, though caution needed if chronic BZD use (seizure risk on reversal).

drugs.indications: Intraoperative/postoperative analgesia (anesthesia adjunct), also see Opioid domain for broader indications
drugs.mechanism: Mu-opioid receptor agonism blunting the sympathetic/hemodynamic response to surgical stimulation and providing intra/postoperative analgesia, reducing volatile anesthetic requirements
drugs.elimination: Renal (active metabolite accumulates in renal impairment)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Synthetic mu-opioid receptor agonist, ~100x more potent than morphine
drugs.indications: Intraoperative analgesia, sedation adjunct, rapid-onset pain management
drugs.route: Intravenous, transdermal, transmucosal (see also Opioid domain)
drugs.mechanism: Highly lipophilic mu-opioid agonist with rapid onset (~1-2 min IV) and short duration due to rapid redistribution (not metabolism) after single doses
sideEffects: Chest wall rigidity (rapid high-dose IV push — 'wooden chest syndrome')
Minimal histamine release (less hypotension than morphine)

dosing.standard: 1-2 mcg/kg IV bolus (analgesia adjunct); higher doses for cardiac anesthesia

drugs.halfLife: ~3.5-7 hours (context-sensitive half-life increases significantly with prolonged infusion, unlike single bolus)

subclass.fr: Opioïde - adjuvant anesthésique (durée ultra-courte, liaison ester)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Synthetic mu-opioid agonist metabolized by plasma/tissue esterases
drugs.indications: Intraoperative analgesia requiring rapid, precise titration and fast offset
drugs.mechanism: Mu-opioid receptor agonism; uniquely metabolized by non-specific plasma and tissue esterases (not hepatic/renal-dependent), giving an extremely predictable, context-insensitive half-life regardless of infusion duration
sideEffects: Acute opioid tolerance/hyperalgesia (notable with this agent, may require multimodal analgesia at emergence)

dosing.frequency: Continuous infusion only (not for bolus-only use given ultra-short duration)

drugs.halfLife: ~3-10 minutes (context-insensitive — does not accumulate regardless of infusion duration)
contraindications: Epidural/intrathecal administration (contains glycine — contraindicated by these routes)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Its context-insensitive half-life (same recovery time whether infused for 10 minutes or 10 hours) makes it uniquely suited for very long or unpredictable-duration procedures.

drugs.therapeuticClass: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent (only one in clinical use)
drugs.indications: Rapid sequence intubation, brief procedures requiring paralysis
drugs.mechanism: Binds nicotinic ACh receptors at the neuromuscular junction, causing sustained depolarization (initial fasciculations followed by flaccid paralysis as the receptor becomes desensitized); rapidly hydrolyzed by plasma pseudocholinesterase, giving the fastest onset/offset of all NMBAs
sideEffects: Hyperkalemia (can be severe/fatal in burns, denervation injury, neuromuscular disease — upregulated extrajunctional receptors)

dosing.maxDose: Single dose typically sufficient given ultra-short duration

contraindications: Hyperkalemia risk states (burns >24h old, denervation injury, prolonged immobilization, neuromuscular disease)
Penetrating eye injury (relative, increases intraocular pressure)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker, intermediate duration, fastest onset of the class
drugs.indications: Rapid sequence intubation (alternative to succinylcholine), maintenance of surgical paralysis
drugs.mechanism: Competitively antagonizes nicotinic ACh receptors at the neuromuscular junction, preventing depolarization; at high (RSI) doses has onset approaching succinylcholine without the hyperkalemia/malignant hyperthermia risk
sideEffects: Anaphylaxis (can occur, cross-reactive with other steroidal NMBAs)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Can be rapidly and completely reversed with sugammadex (a modified cyclodextrin that encapsulates rocuronium), a major advantage over succinylcholine when a difficult airway is unexpectedly encountered.

drugs.indications: Maintenance of surgical paralysis, ICU paralysis (mechanical ventilation)
drugs.mechanism: Competitive nicotinic ACh receptor antagonism at the neuromuscular junction; minimal cardiovascular/histamine-releasing effects
sideEffects: Prolonged paralysis (especially with hepatic/renal impairment, or prolonged ICU infusion — critical illness myopathy risk)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker with unique organ-independent elimination
drugs.indications: Maintenance of surgical paralysis, especially useful in hepatic/renal impairment
drugs.mechanism: Competitive nicotinic ACh receptor antagonism; uniquely undergoes Hofmann elimination (spontaneous, pH/temperature-dependent chemical degradation) and ester hydrolysis, independent of liver/kidney function
sideEffects: Laudanosine accumulation (a Hofmann elimination byproduct, theoretical CNS excitation with prolonged high-dose infusion, rarely clinically significant)
drugs.metabolism: Hofmann elimination (spontaneous, organ-independent) and ester hydrolysis
drugs.elimination: Non-organ-dependent (chemical degradation) — advantageous in organ failure
drugs.clinicalPearls: Preferred NMBA in patients with combined hepatic and renal failure since its elimination does not depend on either organ system.

drugs.therapeuticClass: Non-depolarizing NMBA, single stereoisomer of atracurium
drugs.indications: Maintenance of surgical paralysis, ICU paralysis, organ failure patients
drugs.mechanism: Same Hofmann elimination mechanism as atracurium, but as a purified stereoisomer it produces significantly less histamine release, making it better tolerated hemodynamically
sideEffects: Minimal histamine release (major advantage over atracurium)
Prolonged paralysis in ICU with continuous infusion (rare)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Non-depolarizing NMBA, shortest-acting of the class
drugs.indications: Brief surgical procedures requiring paralysis
drugs.mechanism: Competitive nicotinic ACh receptor antagonism; metabolized by plasma pseudocholinesterase (like succinylcholine), giving the shortest duration among non-depolarizing NMBAs
sideEffects: Prolonged paralysis in pseudocholinesterase deficiency (same concern as succinylcholine)

drugs.indications: Otitis media, sinusitis, pharyngitis, community-acquired pneumonia, UTIs, H. pylori eradication (combination)
drugs.mechanism: Binds penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), inhibiting bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan cross-linking (transpeptidation), causing cell lysis (bactericidal); extended spectrum vs penicillin G covers some Gram-negatives
sideEffects: Rash (notably common if given during mononucleosis)

dosing.standard: 500 mg 3 times daily or 875mg twice daily

contraindications: Mononucleosis (relative — high rash incidence, not true allergy)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Aminopenicillin combined with a beta-lactamase inhibitor
drugs.indications: Same as amoxicillin plus coverage of beta-lactamase-producing organisms (e.g., H. influenzae, some Staph aureus, animal/human bite wounds)
drugs.mechanism: Amoxicillin inhibits cell wall synthesis; clavulanic acid irreversibly inhibits bacterial beta-lactamase enzymes, protecting amoxicillin from degradation and restoring efficacy against resistant strains

dosing.standard: 875/125 mg twice daily or 500/125mg 3 times daily

contraindications: History of amoxicillin-clavulanate-associated cholestatic jaundice/hepatic dysfunction

subclass.fr: Bêta-lactamine - pénicilline résistante à la pénicillinase

drugs.indications: Methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) infections (skin/soft tissue, bone/joint)
drugs.mechanism: Same PBP-binding/cell wall synthesis inhibition as other penicillins, but its bulky side chain sterically hinders staphylococcal penicillinase from hydrolyzing the beta-lactam ring

drugs.therapeuticClass: Extended-spectrum ureidopenicillin combined with a beta-lactamase inhibitor
drugs.indications: Broad-spectrum empiric coverage — nosocomial pneumonia, intra-abdominal infections, febrile neutropenia, sepsis (covers Pseudomonas, anaerobes, many Gram-negatives)
drugs.mechanism: Piperacillin (broad Gram-negative, including Pseudomonas coverage) inhibits cell wall synthesis; tazobactam protects it from beta-lactamase degradation

dosing.standard: 3.375-4.5 g every 6-8 hours (extended infusion often preferred)

drugs.indications: Surgical prophylaxis, skin/soft tissue infections, MSSA infections
drugs.mechanism: Binds PBPs inhibiting cell wall synthesis (same mechanism as penicillins), with a spectrum favoring Gram-positive cocci and modest Gram-negative coverage

dosing.standard: 1-2 g every 8 hours; 2g single dose (surgical prophylaxis)

drugs.clinicalPearls: The standard surgical prophylaxis antibiotic given its reliable Gram-positive (skin flora) coverage and excellent tissue penetration.

drugs.therapeuticClass: Third-generation cephalosporin (broad Gram-negative coverage, CNS penetration)
drugs.indications: Community-acquired pneumonia, meningitis, gonorrhea, pyelonephritis, sepsis (empiric)
drugs.mechanism: PBP binding/cell wall synthesis inhibition with expanded Gram-negative spectrum and good CSF penetration (crosses inflamed meninges), unlike earlier-generation cephalosporins
sideEffects: Biliary sludging/pseudolithiasis (unique to ceftriaxone, calcium-ceftriaxone precipitates)
Kernicterus risk in neonates with hyperbilirubinemia (displaces bilirubin from albumin — avoid in neonates)
drugs.elimination: Renal and biliary (dual route, unique among cephalosporins)
contraindications: Concurrent IV calcium-containing solutions in neonates (fatal precipitation risk)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Fourth-generation cephalosporin (broadest Gram-negative including Pseudomonas, plus Gram-positive coverage)
drugs.indications: Febrile neutropenia, nosocomial pneumonia, complicated UTIs, empiric coverage of Pseudomonas
drugs.mechanism: Same PBP mechanism; zwitterionic structure allows rapid penetration through Gram-negative outer membrane porins, providing balanced broad Gram-positive AND Gram-negative (including Pseudomonas) coverage
sideEffects: Neurotoxicity/encephalopathy (notable, especially in renal impairment with inadequate dose adjustment)
contraindications: Requires significant dose adjustment in renal impairment (neurotoxicity risk if not adjusted)

drugs.indications: Severe/complicated infections, multidrug-resistant organisms (ESBL-producers), empiric therapy in critically ill/septic patients
drugs.mechanism: PBP binding/cell wall synthesis inhibition with the broadest spectrum of any beta-lactam class (Gram-positive, Gram-negative including Pseudomonas, and anaerobes), and stability against most beta-lactamases including ESBLs
sideEffects: Seizures (lower risk than imipenem but still present, especially in renal impairment/high doses)
drugs.metabolism: Minimal metabolism (does not require cilastatin, unlike imipenem)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Reserved as a 'last-line' broad-spectrum agent for resistant organisms — overuse drives carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE), a major antimicrobial resistance concern.

drugs.therapeuticClass: Carbapenem combined with a renal dehydropeptidase inhibitor
drugs.indications: Severe/complicated infections, multidrug-resistant organisms
drugs.mechanism: Imipenem inhibits cell wall synthesis (broadest beta-lactam spectrum); cilastatin inhibits renal dehydropeptidase-I, which would otherwise rapidly degrade imipenem in the kidney before it can act
sideEffects: Seizures (higher risk than meropenem, particularly with renal impairment/high doses/CNS disease)
contraindications: Seizure disorder (relative — meropenem preferred if CNS pathology present)

drugs.indications: MRSA infections, severe Gram-positive infections (bacteremia, endocarditis), C. difficile colitis (oral formulation only)
drugs.route: Intravenous, oral (for C. diff only — not absorbed systemically)
drugs.mechanism: Binds the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors, sterically blocking transglycosylation/transpeptidation and preventing cell wall synthesis — a different binding site than beta-lactams, explaining lack of cross-resistance
sideEffects: Red man syndrome (histamine-mediated infusion reaction, NOT a true allergy — managed by slowing infusion)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Red man syndrome is prevented by infusing over at least 60 minutes and pre-treating with antihistamines if recurrent — it is a rate-related histamine release, not a true drug allergy.

drugs.indications: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE), MRSA (alternative to vancomycin, better lung penetration), complicated skin/soft tissue infections
drugs.mechanism: Binds the 23S rRNA of the 50S ribosomal subunit, blocking formation of the initiation complex for protein synthesis — a unique binding site distinct from other protein synthesis inhibitors, avoiding cross-resistance
sideEffects: Thrombocytopenia/myelosuppression (dose/duration-dependent, requires monitoring with prolonged use)
Serotonin syndrome (weak MAO inhibitor — caution with SSRIs/SNRIs)
contraindications: Concurrent MAOI use or within 2 weeks
Uncontrolled hypertension/pheochromocytoma/carcinoid syndrome (relative, due to weak MAO inhibition)

drugs.indications: Complicated UTIs, pyelonephritis, intra-abdominal infections, anthrax (post-exposure prophylaxis)
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, preventing DNA supercoiling/replication — bactericidal
sideEffects: Tendon rupture/tendinopathy (black box, especially Achilles, with concurrent corticosteroids or in elderly)
drugs.metabolism: Hepatic (minimal, CYP1A2 inhibitor itself — significant theophylline/caffeine interactions)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Multiple FDA black box warnings (tendon rupture, neuropathy, CNS effects, aortic dissection, myasthenia exacerbation) have shifted fluoroquinolones from first-line to reserve status for many indications.

drugs.indications: Community-acquired pneumonia, sinusitis, complicated UTIs
drugs.mechanism: Same DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV inhibition, with improved activity against Streptococcus pneumoniae and atypical pathogens (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella) compared to ciprofloxacin

drugs.indications: Community-acquired pneumonia, atypical pathogens (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella), pertussis, chlamydia (STI), traveler's diarrhea
drugs.mechanism: Binds the 50S ribosomal subunit (23S rRNA), blocking translocation during protein synthesis (bacteriostatic); exceptionally long tissue half-life allows short-course dosing ('Z-pack')
sideEffects: QT prolongation (notable, torsades risk especially with other QT-prolonging drugs)
Cardiovascular death risk signal (controversial epidemiologic data)
drugs.metabolism: Hepatic (minimal, not a significant CYP3A4 inhibitor unlike erythromycin/clarithromycin)

drugs.indications: H. pylori eradication (combination therapy), community-acquired pneumonia, Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC), sinusitis
drugs.mechanism: Same 50S ribosomal binding mechanism as azithromycin; potent CYP3A4 inhibition creates significant drug interaction potential (unlike azithromycin)
sideEffects: Significant CYP3A4-mediated drug interactions (statins, warfarin, etc.)
drugs.metabolism: Hepatic (CYP3A4 — both substrate and potent inhibitor)
contraindications: Concurrent CYP3A4 substrates with narrow therapeutic index (e.g., colchicine, ergotamines, certain statins)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Lincosamide (anaerobic and Gram-positive coverage, good tissue/bone penetration)
drugs.indications: Anaerobic infections, aspiration pneumonia, skin/soft tissue infections (including some MRSA), toxin suppression in necrotizing fasciitis/toxic shock (adjunct)
drugs.mechanism: Binds the 50S ribosomal subunit blocking protein synthesis (same binding region as macrolides, causing cross-resistance in some strains); at the toxin-producing stage of infection, also suppresses bacterial exotoxin production independent of bacterial killing
sideEffects: C. difficile colitis (one of the highest-risk antibiotics for this — classic association)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Added to beta-lactams in necrotizing fasciitis/toxic shock syndrome specifically for its toxin-suppression effect (via protein synthesis inhibition), not just for additional bacterial killing.

drugs.indications: Anaerobic infections, C. difficile colitis (alternative to vancomycin), bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, amebiasis, giardiasis
drugs.mechanism: Reduced intracellularly by anaerobic organisms' electron transport proteins, forming reactive nitroso radical intermediates that damage bacterial/protozoal DNA — requires an anaerobic environment for activation, hence its selectivity for anaerobes
sideEffects: Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol (avoid during and 3 days after treatment)

subclass.fr: Association sulfamide + inhibiteur de la synthèse du folate

drugs.therapeuticClass: Sequential folate synthesis pathway blockade (synergistic combination)
drugs.indications: Uncomplicated UTIs, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (treatment and prophylaxis), MRSA skin infections, Stenotrophomonas infections
drugs.mechanism: Sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase; trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase — sequential blockade of the same folate synthesis pathway at two steps produces synergistic bactericidal activity
sideEffects: Hyperkalemia (trimethoprim, amiloride-like effect on renal tubule)

dosing.maxDose: Higher doses for PCP treatment (15-20mg/kg/day trimethoprim component)
dosing.frequency: Twice daily (standard); more frequent for PCP treatment

drugs.halfLife: ~8-11 hours (both components similar, by design for synergy)

drugs.indications: Severe Gram-negative infections (synergy with beta-lactams for endocarditis), sepsis (empiric, combination therapy)
drugs.mechanism: Binds the 30S ribosomal subunit causing misreading of mRNA and defective protein synthesis; requires oxygen-dependent uptake (ineffective against anaerobes); concentration-dependent killing (once-daily high-dose dosing strategy commonly used)
sideEffects: Ototoxicity (vestibular and cochlear, can be irreversible)

dosing.standard: 5-7 mg/kg once daily (extended-interval dosing) or 1-2.5mg/kg every 8h
dosing.frequency: Once daily (preferred) or every 8h, dosed by levels

contraindications: Pre-existing significant renal impairment/hearing loss (relative, requires careful risk-benefit)

drugs.indications: Community-acquired pneumonia (atypicals), Lyme disease, chlamydia, rickettsial infections, acne, malaria prophylaxis
drugs.mechanism: Binds the 30S ribosomal subunit, blocking aminoacyl-tRNA attachment and preventing protein synthesis (bacteriostatic); broad spectrum including atypicals and some protozoa (malaria prophylaxis)
sideEffects: Tooth discoloration/enamel hypoplasia (children <8 years, pregnancy — contraindicated)
Esophagitis (take with adequate water, remain upright)
drugs.elimination: Fecal (primary, unlike other tetracyclines which are more renal-dependent — safer in renal impairment)
contraindications: Children <8 years (relative, short courses sometimes used for specific indications like anthrax/Lyme)

drugs.indications: Lymphomas, leukemias, breast cancer, autoimmune diseases (lupus nephritis, vasculitis)
drugs.mechanism: Prodrug activated hepatically to phosphoramide mustard, which cross-links DNA strands, preventing replication and causing cell death (cell-cycle nonspecific)
sideEffects: Hemorrhagic cystitis (acrolein metabolite — mitigated by mesna and hydration)
drugs.metabolism: Hepatic (CYP2B6/3A4, activation to phosphoramide mustard and toxic acrolein)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Mesna is co-administered to bind and detoxify acrolein in the bladder, preventing hemorrhagic cystitis.

drugs.indications: Testicular, ovarian, bladder, lung, head/neck cancers
drugs.mechanism: Forms intrastrand and interstrand DNA cross-links (platinum-DNA adducts), disrupting replication/transcription and triggering apoptosis

dosing.maxDose: Per protocol, cumulative dose limited by neuro/nephrotoxicity

drugs.therapeuticClass: Platinum-based DNA cross-linking agent (better tolerated analog of cisplatin)
drugs.indications: Ovarian, lung cancer
drugs.mechanism: Same DNA cross-linking mechanism as cisplatin, but more stable, releasing the active platinum species more slowly — less nephro/oto/neurotoxic but more myelosuppressive

dosing.standard: Dosed by Calvert formula (AUC-based, using renal function)

contraindications: Significant renal impairment (dosing adjusted via Calvert formula)

drugs.indications: Breast cancer, lymphomas, leukemias, sarcomas
drugs.mechanism: Intercalates between DNA base pairs and inhibits topoisomerase II, causing DNA strand breaks; also generates free radicals contributing to both antitumor effect and cardiotoxicity
sideEffects: Cardiotoxicity (dose-cumulative, dilated cardiomyopathy — black box, lifetime dose limit)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Cardiac monitoring (echocardiogram/MUGA) is required before and during treatment given the cumulative, dose-dependent, often irreversible cardiotoxicity.

drugs.indications: Leukemias, lymphomas, choriocarcinoma, osteosarcoma (high-dose); rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis (low-dose)
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking conversion of folate to its active tetrahydrofolate form, halting purine/pyrimidine synthesis and DNA replication (S-phase specific)

dosing.standard: 7.5-25 mg/week (rheumatoid arthritis, low-dose); high-dose g/m2 protocols in oncology

drugs.halfLife: ~3-10 hours (low dose); up to 27 hours (high dose)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Leucovorin (folinic acid) rescue is used after high-dose methotrexate to 'rescue' normal cells from toxicity while still allowing tumor cell death, since tumor cells often have impaired folate rescue mechanisms.

drugs.indications: Colorectal cancer, breast cancer, pancreatic cancer, topical (actinic keratosis, basal cell carcinoma)
drugs.mechanism: Converted intracellularly to FdUMP, which inhibits thymidylate synthase, blocking thymidine (and thus DNA) synthesis; also incorporated into RNA disrupting its function
sideEffects: DPD deficiency (severe toxicity if enzyme deficient — genetic testing recommended)

dosing.standard: Per protocol (bolus or continuous infusion regimens vary widely)

drugs.indications: Leukemias, lymphomas, sarcomas (often combined in CHOP/similar regimens)
drugs.mechanism: Binds tubulin, preventing microtubule polymerization, arresting cells in metaphase (M-phase specific)
sideEffects: Peripheral neuropathy (dose-limiting, distinctive to this drug — minimal myelosuppression unlike most chemo)
Fatal if given intrathecally (must never be administered this route)

dosing.standard: 1.4 mg/m2 per cycle (capped at 2mg absolute dose)

drugs.clinicalPearls: Accidental intrathecal administration is invariably fatal — a critical medication safety checkpoint in oncology pharmacy practice (vincristine must never be dispensed in a syringe compatible with intrathecal delivery).

drugs.indications: Ovarian, breast, lung cancer, Kaposi sarcoma
drugs.mechanism: Binds and stabilizes microtubules, preventing their normal disassembly, arresting cells in mitosis (M-phase specific) — opposite mechanism to vinca alkaloids but same functional endpoint
contraindications: Severe hypersensitivity to Cremophor EL vehicle

drugs.indications: Breast, lung, prostate, gastric cancer
drugs.mechanism: Same microtubule stabilization mechanism as paclitaxel, with higher potency and a different solubilizing vehicle (polysorbate 80)

drugs.indications: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (maintenance), inflammatory bowel disease (off-label)
drugs.mechanism: Converted to thioinosine monophosphate, inhibiting purine synthesis and incorporating into DNA/RNA, disrupting replication
sideEffects: Myelosuppression (significantly increased in TPMT-deficient patients — genetic testing recommended)
drugs.metabolism: Hepatic (xanthine oxidase, TPMT — genetic polymorphism critical for dosing)
contraindications: TPMT deficiency without dose adjustment (severe myelosuppression risk)
Concurrent allopurinol without dose reduction (allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase, the major clearance pathway, causing toxic accumulation)

drugs.indications: Heart failure (volume overload), pulmonary edema, edema (hepatic/renal), hypertension (adjunct)
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, blocking sodium/chloride reabsorption and producing potent diuresis; most potent diuretic class
drugs.elimination: Renal (secretion into tubule required for action — needs adequate renal function/blood flow)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Loop diuretic (NKCC2 inhibitor, more potent per mg than furosemide)
drugs.indications: Edema (heart failure, hepatic, renal disease)
drugs.mechanism: Same NKCC2 inhibition mechanism as furosemide, but ~40x more potent per milligram with more reliable oral bioavailability
sideEffects: Ototoxicity (lower risk than furosemide at equipotent doses)

drugs.indications: Hypertension (first-line), mild edema, nephrolithiasis prevention (calcium-sparing effect)
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits the Na+-Cl- cotransporter (NCC) in the distal convoluted tubule, producing modest diuresis; also promotes calcium reabsorption (opposite of loop diuretics), useful in calcium-based kidney stone prevention
contraindications: Severe renal impairment (loses efficacy as GFR falls, <30 mL/min)

drugs.indications: Hypertension
drugs.mechanism: Same NCC inhibition mechanism as thiazides, with some additional direct vasodilatory activity contributing to its antihypertensive effect

drugs.therapeuticClass: Thiazide-like diuretic, longest half-life of the class
drugs.indications: Hypertension (evidence-based, ALLHAT trial)
drugs.mechanism: Same NCC inhibition mechanism, with the longest duration of action among thiazide-type diuretics, providing more sustained 24-hour BP control
sideEffects: Hypokalemia (more pronounced than HCTZ due to longer action)

subclass.fr: Diurétique épargneur de potassium - bloqueur du canal ENaC

drugs.indications: Adjunct to other diuretics to prevent hypokalemia, Liddle syndrome
drugs.mechanism: Directly blocks the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) in the collecting duct, reducing sodium reabsorption and secondarily reducing potassium/hydrogen secretion (independent of aldosterone, unlike spironolactone)
sideEffects: Hyperkalemia (main risk, especially with ACEi/ARB/renal impairment)
contraindications: Concurrent potassium supplements/other K+-sparing diuretics (additive hyperkalemia risk)

subclass.fr: Diurétique épargneur de potassium - antagoniste de l'aldostérone

drugs.indications: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (evidence-based, RALES trial), primary hyperaldosteronism, ascites (cirrhosis), resistant hypertension, hirsutism (off-label, antiandrogen effect)
drugs.mechanism: Competitively blocks aldosterone at the mineralocorticoid receptor in the collecting duct, reducing sodium reabsorption/potassium secretion; also has antiandrogen activity (blocks androgen receptors and inhibits testosterone synthesis)
sideEffects: Gynecomastia/menstrual irregularities (antiandrogen effect — notable, unique to spironolactone vs eplerenone)

dosing.standard: 12.5-25 mg once daily (heart failure); up to 400mg/day (hyperaldosteronism)

drugs.clinicalPearls: Gynecomastia is dose-dependent and much more common than with eplerenone (a more selective aldosterone antagonist) due to spironolactone's cross-reactivity with androgen and progesterone receptors.

drugs.indications: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, heart failure (with or without diabetes, HFrEF and HFpEF), chronic kidney disease (nephroprotective, independent of diabetes status)
drugs.mechanism: Blocks SGLT2 in the proximal renal tubule, preventing glucose (and secondarily sodium) reabsorption, causing glucosuria and mild osmotic diuresis; benefits in heart failure/CKD are thought to extend beyond glycemic control alone
sideEffects: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (rare but important — can occur with normal glucose levels)
contraindications: Type 1 diabetes/DKA history (increased euglycemic DKA risk)
Severe renal impairment (efficacy diminished, though cardio/renal-protective benefit may persist at lower eGFR per newer trials)

drugs.indications: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, heart failure (reduction in cardiovascular death — EMPA-REG trial), chronic kidney disease
drugs.mechanism: Same SGLT2 inhibition mechanism as dapagliflozin; landmark EMPA-REG OUTCOME trial demonstrated significant cardiovascular mortality reduction
contraindications: Severe renal impairment/dialysis (per specific product labeling)

drugs.indications: Mild-moderate pain, antitussive (cough suppression)
drugs.mechanism: Prodrug requiring CYP2D6 conversion to morphine for most of its analgesic activity — highly variable efficacy depending on individual CYP2D6 metabolizer status (poor metabolizers get little effect; ultrarapid metabolizers risk toxicity)
sideEffects: Respiratory depression (particularly in CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers, including breastfeeding infant toxicity reports)
drugs.metabolism: Hepatic (CYP2D6 to active morphine; CYP3A4 to inactive norcodeine)
contraindications: Breastfeeding (black box, CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizer risk to infant)

subclass.en: Opioid - weak agonist with monoamine activity (Step II)
subclass.fr: Opioïde - agoniste faible à activité monoaminergique (Palier II)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Weak mu-opioid agonist plus serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake inhibition
drugs.indications: Moderate pain
drugs.mechanism: Dual mechanism: weak mu-opioid agonism (active metabolite O-desmethyltramadol via CYP2D6 is more potent) plus serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibition, contributing additional non-opioid analgesia
contraindications: Concurrent MAOI use or within 14 days

drugs.therapeuticClass: Full mu-opioid receptor agonist (prototype strong opioid)
drugs.indications: Severe acute/chronic pain, cancer pain, dyspnea (palliative), acute pulmonary edema (adjunct)
drugs.mechanism: Full agonist at mu-opioid receptors (also kappa/delta to lesser extent), producing analgesia, euphoria, sedation, and respiratory depression via central and spinal mechanisms
sideEffects: Constipation (does not develop tolerance, unlike other effects)

dosing.standard: Individualized, no ceiling effect — titrate to analgesia/side effects
dosing.maxDose: No absolute ceiling (limited by side effects)

drugs.elimination: Renal (active metabolite accumulates significantly in renal impairment — dose adjustment critical)

drugs.indications: Moderate-severe acute/chronic pain
drugs.mechanism: Same full mu-agonist mechanism as morphine, with higher oral bioavailability and somewhat different receptor binding profile (some evidence of kappa-receptor contribution)
sideEffects: High abuse/diversion potential (notable in the opioid epidemic context)

dosing.maxDose: No absolute ceiling (titrate to effect/side effects)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Full mu-opioid receptor agonist (synthetic, ~100x morphine potency)
drugs.indications: Chronic severe pain requiring around-the-clock opioid therapy (transdermal), breakthrough cancer pain (transmucosal)
drugs.mechanism: Full mu-opioid agonism; transdermal formulation provides a depot effect through the skin allowing 72-hour dosing intervals, requiring opioid tolerance before initiation
sideEffects: Respiratory depression (particularly dangerous with heat exposure, accelerating transdermal absorption)
Major contributor to illicit opioid overdose deaths (as illicitly manufactured fentanyl, distinct from the pharmaceutical formulations discussed here)
drugs.halfLife: ~17-24 hours (transdermal, due to skin depot effect)
contraindications: Opioid-naive patients (transdermal — black box, only for opioid-tolerant patients)
Acute/postoperative pain (transdermal formulation contraindicated for this use)
drugs.clinicalPearls: External heat sources (fever, heating pads, hot baths) can dangerously accelerate transdermal fentanyl absorption, precipitating fatal respiratory depression — patients must be counseled to avoid heat exposure over the patch.

subclass.en: Opioid - strong agonist (Step III, synthetic, long-acting)
subclass.fr: Opioïde - agoniste fort (Palier III, synthétique, longue durée)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Full mu-opioid agonist with NMDA antagonist activity, very long and variable half-life
drugs.indications: Opioid use disorder (maintenance treatment), chronic severe pain
drugs.mechanism: Full mu-opioid agonism plus NMDA receptor antagonism (contributing to efficacy in neuropathic pain and reduced tolerance development), with an exceptionally long and unpredictable half-life leading to drug accumulation risk
sideEffects: Respiratory depression (delayed onset relative to analgesic effect — major overdose risk during dose titration)

dosing.standard: Highly individualized, very slow titration (pain); per opioid treatment program protocol (addiction)
dosing.frequency: Once daily typically, given long half-life

drugs.halfLife: ~8-59 hours (extremely variable between individuals — a major source of accumulation/overdose risk)
contraindications: Congenital long QT syndrome (relative, requires baseline/monitoring ECG)
drugs.clinicalPearls: The mismatch between its short analgesic duration and much longer elimination half-life is the classic cause of delayed, cumulative overdose when titrated too quickly for pain — a critical safety teaching point.

drugs.therapeuticClass: Partial mu-opioid receptor agonist, kappa antagonist
drugs.indications: Opioid use disorder (maintenance treatment), chronic pain (transdermal)
drugs.mechanism: High-affinity partial mu-agonist with a 'ceiling effect' on respiratory depression (safer overdose profile than full agonists) and very slow receptor dissociation, which also displaces/blocks other opioids if taken concurrently (precipitating withdrawal if given too soon after full agonist use)
sideEffects: Precipitated withdrawal (if administered too soon after a full opioid agonist)
Respiratory depression (ceiling effect, but still risk especially with benzodiazepines)

dosing.standard: Induction 2-4 mg sublingual, titrate to 8-24mg/day (OUD maintenance)

drugs.clinicalPearls: Must be started only after the patient is in mild-moderate withdrawal from full agonists (to avoid precipitated withdrawal) — a key practical challenge in OUD induction protocols.

drugs.indications: Moderate-severe pain (particularly obstetric analgesia), reversal of opioid-induced pruritus
drugs.mechanism: Agonizes kappa-opioid receptors (analgesia, sedation) while antagonizing mu-receptors, giving a ceiling effect on respiratory depression and reduced abuse potential compared to full mu-agonists — but can precipitate withdrawal in mu-agonist-dependent patients
sideEffects: Dysphoria (kappa-agonist related, notable at higher doses)
contraindications: Concurrent full mu-agonist opioid dependence (precipitated withdrawal)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Pure competitive opioid receptor antagonist (all subtypes)
drugs.indications: Opioid overdose reversal (respiratory depression)
drugs.mechanism: Competitively displaces opioid agonists from mu (and other) receptors with high affinity but no intrinsic activity, rapidly reversing respiratory depression and sedation
sideEffects: Acute opioid withdrawal (in opioid-dependent patients — agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, vomiting)
Recurrence of respiratory depression as naloxone wears off before longer-acting opioids (requires repeat dosing/monitoring)

dosing.standard: 0.4-2 mg IV/IM/IN, repeat every 2-3 min as needed
dosing.maxDose: 10 mg cumulative (consider alternative diagnosis if no response)
dosing.frequency: As needed, may require repeated doses/infusion

drugs.halfLife: ~30-80 minutes (often shorter than the opioid being reversed, requiring re-dosing or infusion)
contraindications: None absolute in a true overdose emergency
drugs.clinicalPearls: Its short half-life relative to longer-acting opioids (methadone, extended-release formulations, fentanyl) means patients require extended monitoring and often repeat dosing/infusion after initial reversal.

drugs.therapeuticClass: Pure competitive opioid receptor antagonist, long-acting
drugs.indications: Opioid use disorder (relapse prevention, after detoxification), alcohol use disorder
drugs.mechanism: Same pure competitive antagonism as naloxone, but with much higher oral bioavailability and longer duration, used prophylactically (not for acute overdose reversal) to block the euphoric/reinforcing effects of opioids or reduce alcohol craving
sideEffects: Precipitated withdrawal (if given before adequate opioid-free interval — must confirm abstinence first, often via naloxone challenge)

dosing.standard: 50 mg once daily (oral) or 380mg IM once monthly (depot)

drugs.halfLife: ~4 hours (parent); ~13 hours (active metabolite); much longer with depot
contraindications: Current opioid use/dependence without adequate washout (7-10 days minimum, precipitated withdrawal risk)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Patients must be opioid-free for at least 7-10 days before starting to avoid precipitated withdrawal — this washout requirement is a major barrier to treatment initiation compared to buprenorphine.

subclass.fr: Antiarythmique - Classe IA (bloqueur des canaux Na+)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Class IA antiarrhythmic (moderate Na+ blockade, also K+ channel blockade)
drugs.indications: Atrial fibrillation/flutter (rhythm control, less common today), ventricular arrhythmias
drugs.mechanism: Blocks fast Na+ channels (intermediate dissociation kinetics) slowing phase 0 depolarization, plus K+ channel blockade prolonging repolarization/QT interval
drugs.metabolism: Hepatic (CYP3A4; also a potent CYP2D6 inhibitor)

subclass.fr: Antiarythmique - Classe IB (bloqueur des canaux Na+)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Class IB antiarrhythmic (fast Na+ channel blockade, preferential for ischemic/depolarized tissue)
drugs.indications: Ventricular arrhythmias (particularly ischemia-related, post-MI VT/VF)
drugs.mechanism: Blocks fast Na+ channels with rapid on/off kinetics, preferentially binding to channels in depolarized/ischemic tissue (use-dependence), suppressing abnormal automaticity while minimally affecting normal conduction
sideEffects: CNS toxicity (dose-dependent — perioral numbness, tinnitus, seizures at high levels)

subclass.fr: Antiarythmique - Classe IC (bloqueur des canaux Na+)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Class IC antiarrhythmic (potent Na+ blockade, slow dissociation)
drugs.indications: Atrial fibrillation (paroxysmal, 'pill-in-the-pocket' approach), supraventricular tachycardia — restricted to patients without structural heart disease
drugs.mechanism: Potent Na+ channel blockade with slow dissociation kinetics, markedly slowing conduction velocity throughout the heart; the CAST trial demonstrated increased mortality when used in patients with structural heart disease/post-MI
sideEffects: Proarrhythmia (increased mortality in structural heart disease — black box, CAST trial)
contraindications: Structural heart disease/prior MI (black box — CAST trial mortality signal)
drugs.clinicalPearls: The landmark CAST trial (1989) showing increased mortality with Class IC agents post-MI fundamentally reshaped antiarrhythmic drug use — now restricted to patients with structurally normal hearts.

drugs.indications: Local/regional anesthesia (largely superseded by amide-type agents)
drugs.mechanism: Blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels on nerve membranes, preventing action potential propagation and producing reversible local sensory (and motor, at higher concentrations) blockade
sideEffects: Allergic reactions (esters metabolized to PABA, a known allergen — higher allergy rate than amides)

drugs.indications: Regional/epidural/spinal anesthesia, postoperative pain control (long-acting nerve blocks), labor epidural analgesia
drugs.route: Local infiltration, epidural, intrathecal, peripheral nerve block
drugs.mechanism: Same Na+ channel blockade mechanism, high potency and long duration of action due to high protein binding and lipid solubility; amide structure metabolized hepatically (not by esterases), lower allergy incidence than esters
sideEffects: Cardiotoxicity (notable — high potency for cardiac Na+ channel blockade, can cause refractory cardiac arrest if injected intravascularly, historically more dangerous than other local anesthetics)
contraindications: IV regional anesthesia (Bier block — contraindicated due to cardiotoxicity risk if tourniquet fails)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Intralipid (lipid emulsion) infusion is the specific treatment for local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), particularly important for bupivacaine given its severe cardiotoxicity profile.

subclass.fr: Anesthésique local - amino-amide (longue durée, profil plus sûr)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Amide-type local anesthetic, developed as a safer alternative to bupivacaine
drugs.indications: Regional/epidural anesthesia, postoperative pain control, labor epidural analgesia
drugs.route: Local infiltration, epidural, peripheral nerve block
drugs.mechanism: Same Na+ channel blockade mechanism as bupivacaine, but formulated as a single (S-) enantiomer, giving less cardiotoxicity and a degree of differential sensory-motor blockade (relatively more sensory than motor block at lower concentrations) — advantageous for labor analgesia
sideEffects: Cardiotoxicity (present but significantly less than bupivacaine)

drugs.therapeuticClass: Amide-type local anesthetic, most widely used local anesthetic overall
drugs.indications: Local infiltration anesthesia, regional nerve blocks, topical anesthesia, IV regional anesthesia (Bier block)
drugs.route: Local infiltration, topical, epidural, intravenous (regional block)
drugs.mechanism: Same Na+ channel blockade mechanism, intermediate potency/duration, favorable safety profile making it the most versatile and commonly used local anesthetic
sideEffects: CNS toxicity at high doses (perioral numbness progressing to seizures)
Methemoglobinemia (rare, with very high doses/prilocaine co-formulations)
drugs.clinicalPearls: The safest and most versatile local anesthetic, used across nearly every route of administration — the benchmark against which other local anesthetics' safety profiles are compared.

subclass.fr: Inhibiteur de la pompe à sodium - digitalique

drugs.indications: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (symptom control, not mortality benefit), atrial fibrillation (rate control, particularly with concurrent HF)
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits the myocardial Na+/K+-ATPase pump, increasing intracellular Na+, which secondarily reduces the activity of the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, raising intracellular Ca2+ and increasing myocardial contractility (positive inotropy); also increases vagal tone, slowing AV nodal conduction
sideEffects: Digoxin toxicity (narrow therapeutic index — nausea, visual disturbances/'yellow-green halos', arrhythmias including the classic bidirectional VT)
Hyperkalemia in acute overdose (paradoxically, from pump inhibition)

dosing.maxDose: 0.25 mg/day (higher doses rarely add benefit, increase toxicity)

drugs.elimination: Renal, largely unchanged — requires significant dose adjustment in renal impairment
contraindications: Hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia (increases toxicity risk, correct before use)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Digoxin immune Fab (DigiFab) is the specific antidote for severe toxicity, binding and neutralizing digoxin molecules — hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia significantly potentiate toxicity risk even at 'therapeutic' digoxin levels.

subclass.fr: Inhibiteur de la pompe à protons

drugs.indications: GERD, peptic ulcer disease, H. pylori eradication (combination), Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
drugs.mechanism: Prodrug activated in the acidic environment of the gastric parietal cell canaliculus, where it irreversibly binds and inhibits the H+/K+-ATPase ('proton pump'), the final common step of acid secretion — new pump synthesis is required to restore acid secretion
drugs.metabolism: Hepatic (CYP2C19, 3A4 — significant genetic polymorphism in CYP2C19 affects levels)
drugs.halfLife: ~0.5-1 hour (but pharmacodynamic effect lasts 24+ hours due to irreversible pump binding)

subclass.fr: Inhibiteur de la pompe à protons

drugs.indications: GERD, peptic ulcer disease, stress ulcer prophylaxis (ICU, IV form commonly used)
drugs.mechanism: Same irreversible H+/K+-ATPase inhibition mechanism; considered to have the fewest CYP450-mediated drug interactions of the PPI class

subclass.fr: Inhibiteur de la pompe à protons (énantiomère unique)

drugs.indications: GERD, peptic ulcer disease, H. pylori eradication
drugs.mechanism: Same mechanism as omeprazole; the S-enantiomer undergoes slower hepatic clearance, giving somewhat higher/more consistent bioavailability and acid suppression compared to racemic omeprazole

subclass.fr: Inhibiteur de la pompe à protons

drugs.indications: GERD, peptic ulcer disease, H. pylori eradication
drugs.mechanism: Same irreversible proton pump inhibition mechanism as other PPIs

drugs.therapeuticClass: Mucosal protective agent (aluminum sucrose sulfate complex)
drugs.indications: Peptic ulcer disease (healing/maintenance), stress ulcer prophylaxis
drugs.mechanism: In an acidic environment, polymerizes and forms a viscous paste that adheres selectively to ulcer craters/damaged mucosa, creating a physical barrier against acid/pepsin/bile — does not directly reduce acid secretion
sideEffects: Reduced absorption of concurrently administered drugs (binds many drugs, requires spaced dosing)

dosing.standard: 1 g 4 times daily (before meals and at bedtime)
dosing.frequency: 4 times daily, on an empty stomach

drugs.clinicalPearls: Must be dosed separately (2 hours apart) from other oral medications since it can physically bind and reduce absorption of many co-administered drugs.
